   207  (ii) the functions of the Director of the Office of Management and Budget

   210                      (b) This order shall be implemented consistent with 
   211                  applicable law and subject to the availability of 
   212                  appropriations.

   214                  create any right or benefit, substantive or procedural,

    28                  Proclamation 10947 of June 3, 2025
    29  
    30                  
    31  Adjusting Imports of Aluminum and Steel Into the 
    32                  United States
    33  
    34                  By the President of the United States of America
    35  
    36                  A Proclamation
    37  
    38                  1. On January 11, 2018, the Secretary of Commerce 
    39                  (Secretary) transmitted to me a report on the 
    40                  Secretary's investigation into the effect of imports of 
    41                  steel mill articles (steel articles) on the national 
    42                  security of the United States under section 232 of the 
    43                  Trade Expansion Act of 1962, as amended (19 U.S.C. 
    44                  1862) (section 232). The Secretary found and advised me 
    45                  of his opinion that steel articles are being imported 
    46                  into the United States in such quantities and under 
    47                  such circumstances as to threaten to impair the 
    48                  national security of the United States.
    49  
    50                  2. In Proclamation 9705 of March 8, 2018 (Adjusting 
    51                  Imports of Steel Into the United States), and 
    52                  Proclamation 9980 of January 24, 2020 (Adjusting 
    53                  Imports of Derivative Aluminum Articles and Derivative 
    54                  Steel Articles Into the United States), I concurred 
    55                  with the Secretary's findings that steel articles, as 
    56                  defined in clause 1 of Proclamation 9705, and 
    57                  derivative steel articles, as described in clause 3 of 
    58                  Proclamation 9980, are being imported into the United 
    59                  States in such quantities and under such circumstances 
    60                  as to threaten to impair the national security of the 
    61                  United States, and I decided to adjust the imports of 
    62                  those steel articles and derivative steel articles by 
    63                  imposing a 25 percent ad valorem tariff on such 
    64                  articles imported from most countries. In Proclamation 
    65                  10896 of February 10, 2025 (Adjusting Imports of Steel 
    66                  Into the United States), I decided to adjust the 
    67                  imports of steel articles and derivative steel articles 
    68                  by imposing a 25 percent ad valorem tariff on such 
    69                  articles imported from all countries.
    70  
    71                  3. On January 19, 2018, the Secretary transmitted to me 
    72                  a report on the Secretary's investigation into the 
    73                  effect of imports of aluminum articles on the national 
    74                  security of the United States under section 232. The 
    75                  Secretary found and advised me of his opinion that 
    76                  aluminum articles are being imported into the United 
    77                  States in such quantities and under such circumstances 
    78                  as to threaten to impair the national security of the 
    79                  United States.
    80  
    81                  4. In Proclamation 9704 of March 8, 2018 (Adjusting 
    82                  Imports of Aluminum Into the United States), and 
    83                  Proclamation 9980, I concurred with the Secretary's 
    84                  findings that aluminum articles, as defined in clause 1 
    85                  of Proclamation 9704, and derivative aluminum articles, 
    86                  as described in clause 3 of Proclamation 9980, are 
    87                  being imported into the United States in such 
    88                  quantities and under such circumstances as to threaten 
    89                  to impair the national security of the United States, 
    90                  and decided to adjust the imports of aluminum articles 
    91                  and derivative aluminum articles by imposing a 10 
    92                  percent ad valorem tariff on such articles imported 
    93                  from most countries. In Proclamation 10895 of February 
    94                  10, 2025 (Adjusting Imports of Aluminum Into the United 
    95                  States), I decided to adjust the imports of aluminum 
    96                  articles and derivative aluminum articles by imposing a 
    97                  25 percent ad valorem tariff on such articles imported 
    98                  from all countries.
    99  
   100                  5. In Proclamation 10896 and Proclamation 10895, I 
   101                  instructed the Secretary to continue to monitor imports 
   102                  of steel articles and derivative steel articles, and 
   103                  aluminum articles and derivative aluminum articles, 
   104                  respectively, and
   105  
   106  [[Page 24200]]
   107  
   108                  to review the status of such imports with respect to 
   109                  the national security of the United States. The 
   110                  Secretary has done so and has advised me accordingly.
   111  
   112                  6. After considering current information newly provided 
   113                  by the Secretary, among other things, I have determined 
   114                  that it is necessary to increase the previously 
   115                  described steel and aluminum tariffs to adjust the 
   116                  imports of steel and aluminum articles and their 
   117                  derivative articles so that such imports will not 
   118                  threaten to impair the national security. In my 
   119                  judgment, the increased tariffs will more effectively 
   120                  counter foreign countries that continue to offload low-
   121                  priced, excess steel and aluminum in the United States 
   122                  market and thereby undercut the competitiveness of the 
   123                  United States steel and aluminum industries. Although 
   124                  the previously imposed steel and aluminum tariffs have 
   125                  helped provide critical price support in the United 
   126                  States market, they have not yet enabled these 
   127                  industries to develop and maintain the rates of 
   128                  capacity production utilization that are necessary for 
   129                  the industries' sustained health and for projected 
   130                  national defense needs. I have determined that 
   131                  increasing the previously imposed tariffs will provide 
   132                  greater support to these industries and reduce or 
   133                  eliminate the national security threat posed by imports 
   134                  of steel and aluminum articles and their derivative 
   135                  articles.
   136  
   137                  7. Accordingly, I have determined that it is necessary 
   138                  and appropriate to increase the tariff rate for imports 
   139                  of steel articles and derivative steel articles, and 
   140                  aluminum articles and derivative aluminum articles, 
   141                  from 25 percent ad valorem to 50 percent ad valorem 
   142                  effective as of 12:01 a.m. eastern daylight time on 
   143                  June 4, 2025. I have also determined that it is 
   144                  necessary and appropriate to modify the way in which 
   145                  the tariff measures described in Executive Order 14289 
   146                  of April 29, 2025 (Addressing Certain Tariffs on 
   147                  Imported Articles), apply to steel articles and 
   148                  derivative steel articles, and aluminum articles and 
   149                  derivative aluminum articles, to ensure the 
   150                  effectiveness of the tariff changes described in this 
   151                  proclamation and the alignment of policy priorities 
   152                  between this proclamation and Executive Order 14289. I 
   153                  have further determined that it is necessary and 
   154                  appropriate to allow for the implementation of the 
   155                  U.S.-UK Economic Prosperity Deal of May 8, 2025 (EPD), 
   156                  and to accordingly provide different treatment, as 
   157                  described below, for imports of steel and aluminum 
   158                  articles, and their derivatives, from the United 
   159                  Kingdom.
   160  
   161                  8. Section 232 authorizes the President to adjust the 
   162                  imports of an article and its derivatives that are 
   163                  being imported into the United States in such 
   164                  quantities or under such circumstances as to threaten 
   165                  to impair the national security.
   166  
   167                  9. Section 604 of the Trade Act of 1974, as amended (19 
   168                  U.S.C. 2483), authorizes the President to embody in the 
   169                  Harmonized Tariff Schedule of the United States (HTSUS) 
   170                  the substance of statutes affecting import treatment, 
   171                  and actions thereunder, including the removal, 
   172                  modification, continuance, or imposition of any rate of 
   173                  duty or other import restriction.
   174  
   175                  NOW, THEREFORE, I, DONALD J. TRUMP, President of the 
   176                  United States of America, by the authority vested in me 
   177                  by the Constitution and the laws of the United States 
   178                  of America, including section 232; the International 
   179                  Emergency Economic Powers Act (50 U.S.C. 1701 et seq.); 
   180                  section 301 of title 3, United States Code; and section 
   181                  604 of the Trade Act of 1974, as amended, do hereby 
   182                  proclaim as follows:
   183  
   184                      (1) As set forth in Annexes I and II to this 
   185                  proclamation, as of 12:01 a.m. eastern daylight time on 
   186                  June 4, 2025, the tariffs proclaimed by Proclamation 
   187                  9704, as amended; Proclamation 9705, as amended; 
   188                  Proclamation 9980, as amended; Proclamation 10895; and 
   189                  Proclamation 10896 are modified to increase the 
   190                  respective tariff rates from an additional 25 percent 
   191                  ad valorem to an additional 50 percent ad valorem.
   192                      (2) The modifications to the HTSUS made by clause 1 
   193                  of this proclamation shall be effective with respect to 
   194                  goods entered for consumption, or withdrawn from 
   195                  warehouse for consumption, on or after 12:01 a.m. 
   196                  eastern
   197  
   198  [[Page 24201]]
   199  
   200                  daylight time on June 4, 2025, and shall continue in 
   201                  effect, unless such actions are expressly reduced, 
   202                  modified, or terminated.
   203                      (3) Any imports of articles set forth in Annex II 
   204                  to this proclamation that were admitted into a United 
   205                  States foreign trade zone under ``privileged foreign 
   206                  status'' as defined in 19 CFR 146.41 before 12:01 a.m. 
   207                  eastern daylight time on June 4, 2025, shall be subject 
   208                  upon entry for consumption made on or after 12:01 a.m. 
   209                  eastern daylight time on June 4, 2025, to the 
   210                  provisions of the tariff in effect at the time of the 
   211                  entry for consumption.
   212                      (4) Any article set forth in Annex I to this 
   213                  proclamation, except those eligible for admission under 
   214                  ``domestic status'' as defined in 19 CFR 146.43, that 
   215                  is subject to a duty imposed by this proclamation and 
   216                  that is admitted into a United States foreign trade 
   217                  zone on or after June 4, 2025, may be admitted only 
   218                  under ``privileged foreign status'' as defined in 19 
   219                  CFR 146.41, and will be subject upon entry for 
   220                  consumption to any ad valorem rates of duty related to 
   221                  the classification under the applicable HTSUS 
   222                  subheading.
   223                      (5) Effective as of 12:01 a.m. eastern daylight 
   224                  time on June 4, 2025, Executive Order 14289 is amended 
   225                  by revising section 3(a)(ii) to read as follows: ``(ii) 
   226                  An article subject to tariffs pursuant to the actions 
   227                  listed in section 2(d) or 2(e) of this order shall not 
   228                  be subject to additional tariffs on that article 
   229                  pursuant to the actions listed in section 2(b) or 2(c) 
   230                  of this order.'' As set forth in Annex III of this 
   231                  proclamation, this amendment shall be effective with 
   232                  respect to goods entered for consumption, or withdrawn 
   233                  from warehouse for consumption, on or after 12:01 a.m. 
   234                  eastern daylight time on June 4, 2025, and shall 
   235                  continue in effect, unless such actions are expressly 
   236                  reduced, modified, or terminated.
   237                      (6) Notwithstanding any prior proclamation or 
   238                  Executive Order, the non-aluminum, non-steel content of 
   239                  all aluminum and steel articles and derivative articles 
   240                  shall be subject to tariffs pursuant to Executive Order 
   241                  14257 of April 2, 2025 (Regulating Imports With a 
   242                  Reciprocal Tariff To Rectify Trade Practices That 
   243                  Contribute to Large and Persistent Annual United States 
   244                  Goods Trade Deficits), as amended, and any other 
   245                  applicable tariffs. The additional ad valorem duties 
   246                  described in clause 1 and clause 7 of this proclamation 
   247                  shall apply only to the steel content of articles in 
   248                  Chapter 73 of the HTSUS and only to the aluminum 
   249                  content of articles in Chapter 76 of the HTSUS. U.S. 
   250                  Customs and Border Protection (CBP) shall issue 
   251                  authoritative guidance mandating strict compliance with 
   252                  declaration requirements for steel and aluminum content 
   253                  in imported articles and outlining maximum penalties 
   254                  for noncompliance, including that importers who submit 
   255                  underreported declarations may be subject to severe 
   256                  consequences, including but not limited to significant 
   257                  monetary penalties, loss of import privileges, and 
   258                  criminal liability, consistent with United States law.
   259                      (7) Notwithstanding clause 1 of this proclamation, 
   260                  the applicable rates of duty for articles of the United 
   261                  Kingdom that would otherwise be applicable pursuant to 
   262                  Proclamation 9704, as amended; Proclamation 9705, as 
   263                  amended; Proclamation 9980, as amended; Proclamation 
   264                  10895; and Proclamation 10896 shall remain at 25 
   265                  percent ad valorem. On or after July 9, 2025, the 
   266                  Secretary may adjust the applicable rates of duty and 
   267                  construct import quotas for steel and aluminum 
   268                  consistent with the terms of the EPD, or he may 
   269                  increase the applicable rates of duty to 50 percent if 
   270                  he determines that the United Kingdom has not complied 
   271                  with relevant aspects of the EPD.
   272                      (8) The Secretary shall continue to monitor imports 
   273                  of the articles and derivative articles described in 
   274                  Annexes I and II to this proclamation, and shall, from 
   275                  time to time, in consultation with any senior executive 
   276                  branch officials the Secretary deems appropriate, 
   277                  review the status of such imports with respect to the 
   278                  national security of the United States. The Secretary 
   279                  shall inform the President of any circumstances that, 
   280                  in the Secretary's opinion, might indicate the need for 
   281                  further action by the President under
   282  
   283  [[Page 24202]]
   284  
   285                  section 232. The Secretary shall also inform the 
   286                  President of any circumstances that, in the Secretary's 
   287                  opinion, might indicate that the duty rate provided for 
   288                  in this proclamation, or any proclamation issued 
   289                  pursuant thereto, is no longer necessary.
   290                      (9) No drawback shall be available with respect to 
   291                  the duties imposed pursuant to this proclamation.
   292                      (10) The Secretary may issue regulations and 
   293                  guidance consistent with this proclamation, including 
   294                  to address operational necessity.
   295                      (11) The Secretary, in consultation with the United 
   296                  States International Trade Commission and CBP, shall 
   297                  determine whether any modifications to the HTSUS are 
   298                  necessary to effectuate this proclamation and may make 
   299                  such modifications through notice in the Federal 
   300                  Register if needed.
   301                      (12) CBP may take any necessary or appropriate 
   302                  measures to administer the tariffs imposed by this 
   303                  proclamation.
   304                      (13) Any provision of previous proclamations and 
   305                  Executive Orders that is inconsistent with the actions 
   306                  taken in this proclamation is superseded to the extent 
   307                  of such inconsistency.
   308  
   309                  IN WITNESS WHEREOF, I have hereunto set my hand this 
   310                  third day of June, in the year of our Lord two thousand 
   311                  twenty-five, and of the Independence of the United 
   312                  States of America the two hundred and forty-ninth.

    57                  Executive Order 14257 of April 2, 2025
    58  
    59                  
    60  Regulating Imports With a Reciprocal Tariff To 
    61                  Rectify Trade Practices That Contribute to Large and 
    62                  Persistent Annual United States Goods Trade Deficits
    63  
    64                  By the authority vested in me as President by the 
    65                  Constitution and the laws of the United States of 
    66                  America, including the International Emergency Economic 
    67                  Powers Act (50 U.S.C. 1701 et seq.)(IEEPA), the 
    68                  National Emergencies Act (50 U.S.C. 1601 et seq.)(NEA), 
    69                  section 604 of the Trade Act of 1974, as amended (19 
    70                  U.S.C. 2483), and section 301 of title 3, United States 
    71                  Code,
    72  
    73                  I, DONALD J. TRUMP, President of the United States of 
    74                  America, find that underlying conditions, including a 
    75                  lack of reciprocity in our bilateral trade 
    76                  relationships, disparate tariff rates and non-tariff 
    77                  barriers, and U.S. trading partners' economic policies 
    78                  that suppress domestic wages and consumption, as 
    79                  indicated by large and persistent annual U.S. goods 
    80                  trade deficits, constitute an unusual and extraordinary 
    81                  threat to the national security and economy of the 
    82                  United States. That threat has its source in whole or 
    83                  substantial part outside the United States in the 
    84                  domestic economic policies of key trading partners and 
    85                  structural imbalances in the global trading system. I 
    86                  hereby declare a national emergency with respect to 
    87                  this threat.
    88  
    89                  On January 20, 2025, I signed the America First Trade 
    90                  Policy Presidential Memorandum directing my 
    91                  Administration to investigate the causes of our 
    92                  country's large and persistent annual trade deficits in 
    93                  goods, including the economic and national security 
    94                  implications and risks resulting from such deficits, 
    95                  and to undertake a review of, and identify, any unfair 
    96                  trade practices by other countries. On February 13, 
    97                  2025, I signed a Presidential Memorandum entitled 
    98                  ``Reciprocal Trade and Tariffs,'' that directed further 
    99                  review of our trading partners' non-reciprocal trading 
   100                  practices, and noted the relationship between non-
   101                  reciprocal practices and the trade deficit. On April 1, 
   102                  2025, I received the final results of those 
   103                  investigations, and I am taking action today based on 
   104                  those results.
   105  
   106                  Large and persistent annual U.S. goods trade deficits 
   107                  have led to the hollowing out of our manufacturing 
   108                  base; inhibited our ability to scale advanced domestic 
   109                  manufacturing capacity; undermined critical supply 
   110                  chains; and rendered our defense-industrial base 
   111                  dependent on foreign adversaries. Large and persistent 
   112                  annual U.S. goods trade deficits are caused in 
   113                  substantial part by a lack of reciprocity in our 
   114                  bilateral trade relationships. This situation is 
   115                  evidenced by disparate tariff rates and non-tariff 
   116                  barriers that make it harder for U.S. manufacturers to 
   117                  sell their products in foreign markets. It is also 
   118                  evidenced by the economic policies of key U.S. trading 
   119                  partners insofar as they suppress domestic wages and 
   120                  consumption, and thereby demand for U.S. exports, while 
   121                  artificially increasing the competitiveness of their 
   122                  goods in global markets. These conditions have given 
   123                  rise to the national emergency that this order is 
   124                  intended to abate and resolve.
   125  
   126                  For decades starting in 1934, U.S. trade policy has 
   127                  been organized around the principle of reciprocity. The 
   128                  Congress directed the President to secure reduced 
   129                  reciprocal tariff rates from key trading partners first 
   130                  through bilateral trade agreements and later under the 
   131                  auspices of the global trading system. Between 1934 and 
   132                  1945, the executive branch negotiated and signed 32 
   133                  bilateral reciprocal trade agreements designed to lower 
   134                  tariff rates on a
   135  
   136  [[Page 15042]]
   137  
   138                  reciprocal basis. After 1947 through 1994, 
   139                  participating countries engaged in eight rounds of 
   140                  negotiation, which resulted in the General Agreements 
   141                  on Tariffs and Trade (GATT) and seven subsequent tariff 
   142                  reduction rounds.
   143  
   144                  However, despite a commitment to the principle of 
   145                  reciprocity, the trading relationship between the 
   146                  United States and its trading partners has become 
   147                  highly unbalanced, particularly in recent years. The 
   148                  post-war international economic system was based upon 
   149                  three incorrect assumptions: first, that if the United 
   150                  States led the world in liberalizing tariff and non-
   151                  tariff barriers the rest of the world would follow; 
   152                  second, that such liberalization would ultimately 
   153                  result in more economic convergence and increased 
   154                  domestic consumption among U.S. trading partners 
   155                  converging towards the share in the United States; and 
   156                  third, that as a result, the United States would not 
   157                  accrue large and persistent goods trade deficits.
   158  
   159                  This framework set in motion events, agreements, and 
   160                  commitments that did not result in reciprocity or 
   161                  generally increase domestic consumption in foreign 
   162                  economies relative to domestic consumption in the 
   163                  United States. Those events, in turn, created large and 
   164                  persistent annual U.S. goods trade deficits as a 
   165                  feature of the global trading system.
   166  
   167                  Put simply, while World Trade Organization (WTO) 
   168                  Members agreed to bind their tariff rates on a most-
   169                  favored-nation (MFN) basis, and thereby provide their 
   170                  best tariff rates to all WTO Members, they did not 
   171                  agree to bind their tariff rates at similarly low 
   172                  levels or to apply tariff rates on a reciprocal basis. 
   173                  Consequently, according to the WTO, the United States 
   174                  has among the lowest simple average MFN tariff rates in 
   175                  the world at 3.3 percent, while many of our key trading 
   176                  partners like Brazil (11.2 percent), China (7.5 
   177                  percent), the European Union (EU) (5 percent), India 
   178                  (17 percent), and Vietnam (9.4 percent) have simple 
   179                  average MFN tariff rates that are significantly higher.
   180  
   181                  Moreover, these average MFN tariff rates conceal much 
   182                  larger discrepancies across economies in tariff rates 
   183                  applied to particular products. For example, the United 
   184                  States imposes a 2.5 percent tariff on passenger 
   185                  vehicle imports (with internal combustion engines), 
   186                  while the European Union (10 percent), India (70 
   187                  percent), and China (15 percent) impose much higher 
   188                  duties on the same product. For network switches and 
   189                  routers, the United States imposes a 0 percent tariff, 
   190                  but for similar products, India (10 percent) levies a 
   191                  higher rate. Brazil (18 percent) and Indonesia (30 
   192                  percent) impose a higher tariff on ethanol than does 
   193                  the United States (2.5 percent). For rice in the husk, 
   194                  the U.S. MFN tariff is 2.7 percent (ad valorem 
   195                  equivalent), while India (80 percent), Malaysia (40 
   196                  percent), and Turkey (an average of 31 percent) impose 
   197                  higher rates. Apples enter the United States duty-free, 
   198                  but not so in Turkey (60.3 percent) and India (50 
   199                  percent).
   200  
   201                  Similarly, non-tariff barriers also deprive U.S. 
   202                  manufacturers of reciprocal access to markets around 
   203                  the world. The 2025 National Trade Estimate Report on 
   204                  Foreign Trade Barriers (NTE) details a great number of 
   205                  non-tariff barriers to U.S. exports around the world on 
   206                  a trading-partner by trading-partner basis. These 
   207                  barriers include import barriers and licensing 
   208                  restrictions; customs barriers and shortcomings in 
   209                  trade facilitation; technical barriers to trade (e.g., 
   210                  unnecessarily trade restrictive standards, conformity 
   211                  assessment procedures, or technical regulations); 
   212                  sanitary and phytosanitary measures that unnecessarily 
   213                  restrict trade without furthering safety objectives; 
   214                  inadequate patent, copyright, trade secret, and 
   215                  trademark regimes and inadequate enforcement of 
   216                  intellectual property rights; discriminatory licensing 
   217                  requirements or regulatory standards; barriers to 
   218                  cross-border data flows and discriminatory practices 
   219                  affecting trade in digital products; investment 
   220                  barriers; subsidies; anticompetitive practices; 
   221                  discrimination in favor of domestic state-owned 
   222                  enterprises, and failures by governments in protecting 
   223                  labor and environment standards; bribery; and 
   224                  corruption.
   225  
   226                  Moreover, non-tariff barriers include the domestic 
   227                  economic policies and practices of our trading 
   228                  partners, including currency practices and value-added 
   229                  taxes, and their associated market distortions, that 
   230                  suppress domestic
   231  
   232  [[Page 15043]]
   233  
   234                  consumption and boost exports to the United States. 
   235                  This lack of reciprocity is apparent in the fact that 
   236                  the share of consumption to Gross Domestic Product 
   237                  (GDP) in the United States is about 68 percent, but it 
   238                  is much lower in others like Ireland (27 percent), 
   239                  Singapore (31 percent), China (39 percent), South Korea 
   240                  (49 percent), and Germany (50 percent).
   241  
   242                  At the same time, efforts by the United States to 
   243                  address these imbalances have stalled. Trading partners 
   244                  have repeatedly blocked multilateral and plurilateral 
   245                  solutions, including in the context of new rounds of 
   246                  tariff negotiations and efforts to discipline non-
   247                  tariff barriers. At the same time, with the U.S. 
   248                  economy disproportionately open to imports, U.S. 
   249                  trading partners have had few incentives to provide 
   250                  reciprocal treatment to U.S. exports in the context of 
   251                  bilateral trade negotiations.
   252  
   253                  These structural asymmetries have driven the large and 
   254                  persistent annual U.S. goods trade deficit. Even for 
   255                  countries with which the United States may enjoy an 
   256                  occasional bilateral trade surplus, the accumulation of 
   257                  tariff and non-tariff barriers on U.S. exports may make 
   258                  that surplus smaller than it would have been without 
   259                  such barriers. Permitting these asymmetries to continue 
   260                  is not sustainable in today's economic and geopolitical 
   261                  environment because of the effect they have on U.S. 
   262                  domestic production. A nation's ability to produce 
   263                  domestically is the bedrock of its national and 
   264                  economic security.
   265  
   266                  Both my first Administration in 2017, and the Biden 
   267                  Administration in 2022, recognized that increasing 
   268                  domestic manufacturing is critical to U.S. national 
   269                  security. According to 2023 United Nations data, U.S. 
   270                  manufacturing output as a share of global manufacturing 
   271                  output was 17.4 percent, down from a peak in 2001 of 
   272                  28.4 percent.
   273  
   274                  Over time, the persistent decline in U.S. manufacturing 
   275                  output has reduced U.S. manufacturing capacity. The 
   276                  need to maintain robust and resilient domestic 
   277                  manufacturing capacity is particularly acute in certain 
   278                  advanced industrial sectors like automobiles, 
   279                  shipbuilding, pharmaceuticals, technology products, 
   280                  machine tools, and basic and fabricated metals, because 
   281                  once competitors gain sufficient global market share in 
   282                  these sectors, U.S. production could be permanently 
   283                  weakened. It is also critical to scale manufacturing 
   284                  capacity in the defense-industrial sector so that we 
   285                  can manufacture the defense materiel and equipment 
   286                  necessary to protect American interests at home and 
   287                  abroad.
   288  
   289                  In fact, because the United States has supplied so much 
   290                  military equipment to other countries, U.S. stockpiles 
   291                  of military goods are too low to be compatible with 
   292                  U.S. national defense interests. Furthermore, U.S. 
   293                  defense companies must develop new, advanced 
   294                  manufacturing technologies across a range of critical 
   295                  sectors including bio-manufacturing, batteries, and 
   296                  microelectronics. If the United States wishes to 
   297                  maintain an effective security umbrella to defend its 
   298                  citizens and homeland, as well as for its allies and 
   299                  partners, it needs to have a large upstream 
   300                  manufacturing and goods-producing ecosystem to 
   301                  manufacture these products without undue reliance on 
   302                  imports for key inputs.
   303  
   304                  Increased reliance on foreign producers for goods also 
   305                  has compromised U.S. economic security by rendering 
   306                  U.S. supply chains vulnerable to geopolitical 
   307                  disruption and supply shocks. In recent years, the 
   308                  vulnerability of the U.S. economy in this respect was 
   309                  exposed both during the COVID-19 pandemic, when 
   310                  Americans had difficulty accessing essential products, 
   311                  as well as when the Houthi rebels later began attacking 
   312                  cargo ships in the Middle East.
   313  
   314                  The decline of U.S. manufacturing capacity threatens 
   315                  the U.S. economy in other ways, including through the 
   316                  loss of manufacturing jobs. From 1997 to 2024, the 
   317                  United States lost around 5 million manufacturing jobs 
   318                  and experienced one of the largest drops in 
   319                  manufacturing employment in history. Furthermore, many 
   320                  manufacturing job losses were concentrated in specific 
   321                  geographical areas. In these areas, the loss of 
   322                  manufacturing jobs contributed
   323  
   324  [[Page 15044]]
   325  
   326                  to the decline in rates of family formation and to the 
   327                  rise of other social trends, like the abuse of opioids, 
   328                  that have imposed profound costs on the U.S. economy.
   329  
   330                  The future of American competitiveness depends on 
   331                  reversing these trends. Today, manufacturing represents 
   332                  just 11 percent of U.S. gross domestic product, yet it 
   333                  accounts for 35 percent of American productivity growth 
   334                  and 60 percent of our exports. Importantly, U.S. 
   335                  manufacturing is the main engine of innovation in the 
   336                  United States, responsible for 55 percent of all 
   337                  patents and 70 percent of all research and development 
   338                  (R&D) spending. The fact that R&D expenditures by U.S. 
   339                  multinational enterprises in China grew at an average 
   340                  rate of 13.6 percent a year between 2003 and 2017, 
   341                  while their R&D expenditures in the United States grew 
   342                  by an average of just 5 percent per year during the 
   343                  same time period, is evidence of the strong link 
   344                  between manufacturing and innovation. Furthermore, 
   345                  every manufacturing job spurs 7 to 12 new jobs in other 
   346                  related industries, helping to build and sustain our 
   347                  economy.
   348  
   349                  Just as a nation that does not produce manufactured 
   350                  products cannot maintain the industrial base it needs 
   351                  for national security, neither can a nation long 
   352                  survive if it cannot produce its own food. Presidential 
   353                  Policy Directive 21 of February 12, 2013 (Critical 
   354                  Infrastructure Security and Resilience), designates 
   355                  food and agriculture as a ``critical infrastructure 
   356                  sector'' because it is one of the sectors considered 
   357                  ``so vital to the United States that [its] incapacity 
   358                  or destruction . . . would have a debilitating impact 
   359                  on security, national economic security, national 
   360                  public health or safety, or any combination of those 
   361                  matters.'' Furthermore, when I left office, the United 
   362                  States had a trade surplus in agricultural products, 
   363                  but today, that surplus has vanished. Eviscerated by a 
   364                  slew of new non-tariff barriers imposed by our trading 
   365                  partners, it has been replaced by a projected $49 
   366                  billion annual agricultural trade deficit.
   367  
   368                  For these reasons, I hereby declare and order:
   369  
   370                  Section 1. National Emergency. As President of the 
   371                  United States, my highest duty is ensuring the national 
   372                  and economic security of the country and its citizens.
   373  
   374                  I have declared a national emergency arising from 
   375                  conditions reflected in large and persistent annual 
   376                  U.S. goods trade deficits, which have grown by over 40 
   377                  percent in the past 5 years alone, reaching $1.2 
   378                  trillion in 2024. This trade deficit reflects 
   379                  asymmetries in trade relationships that have 
   380                  contributed to the atrophy of domestic production 
   381                  capacity, especially that of the U.S. manufacturing and 
   382                  defense-industrial base. These asymmetries also impact 
   383                  U.S. producers' ability to export and, consequentially, 
   384                  their incentive to produce.
   385  
   386                  Specifically, such asymmetry includes not only non-
   387                  reciprocal differences in tariff rates among foreign 
   388                  trading partners, but also extensive use of non-tariff 
   389                  barriers by foreign trading partners, which reduce the 
   390                  competitiveness of U.S. exports while artificially 
   391                  enhancing the competitiveness of their own goods. These 
   392                  non-tariff barriers include technical barriers to 
   393                  trade; non-scientific sanitary and phytosanitary rules; 
   394                  inadequate intellectual property protections; 
   395                  suppressed domestic consumption (e.g., wage 
   396                  suppression); weak labor, environmental, and other 
   397                  regulatory standards and protections; and corruption. 
   398                  These non-tariff barriers give rise to significant 
   399                  imbalances even when the United States and a trading 
   400                  partner have comparable tariff rates.

    65                  Proclamation 11012 of February 20, 2026
    66  
    67                  
    68  Imposing a Temporary Import Surcharge To Address 
    69                  Fundamental International Payments Problems
    70  
    71                  By the President of the United States of America
    72  
    73                  A Proclamation
    74  
    75                  1. The United States plays a pivotal role in shaping 
    76                  the global economy. At the same time, the United States 
    77                  faces various threats to its own economy and national 
    78                  interests. Sometimes, the United States faces 
    79                  fundamental international payments problems, such as 
    80                  large and serious balance-of-payments deficits, an 
    81                  imminent and significant depreciation of its currency 
    82                  in foreign exchange markets, or an international 
    83                  balance-of-payments disequilibrium. These problems can, 
    84                  among other things, endanger the ability of the United 
    85                  States to finance its spending, erode investor 
    86                  confidence in the economy, and distress the financial 
    87                  markets.
    88  
    89                  2. Special import measures to restrict imports, such as 
    90                  surcharges and quotas, are key tools to protect the 
    91                  economy and national security of the United States, 
    92                  and, in certain circumstances, they are required to 
    93                  deal with fundamental international payments problems.
    94  
    95                  3. Given the gravity of fundamental international 
    96                  payments problems and the importance of import 
    97                  restrictions as economic, national security, and 
    98                  foreign policy tools, Federal law, including section 
    99                  122 of the Trade Act of 1974 (19 U.S.C. 2132) (section 
   100                  122), empowers the President to take action through 
   101                  surcharges and other special import restrictions to 
   102                  address fundamental international payments problems.
   103  
   104                  4. I have received certain requested information and 
   105                  opinions from senior officials on whether any 
   106                  fundamental international payments problems exist and 
   107                  the extent to which such problems could impair United 
   108                  States national interests, including economic and 
   109                  national security interests. The information and 
   110                  opinions discuss, among other things, the state of the 
   111                  balance of payments of the United States, the standing 
   112                  of the United States dollar in foreign exchange 
   113                  markets, and the state of international balances of 
   114                  payments. I have also received opinions and 
   115                  recommendations from senior officials on whether 
   116                  special import measures to restrict imports are 
   117                  required to address any fundamental international 
   118                  payments problems. These opinions address, among other 
   119                  things, whether a surcharge in the form of ad valorem 
   120                  duties is required to restrict imports to deal with 
   121                  large and serious United States balance-of-payments 
   122                  deficits, to prevent an imminent and significant 
   123                  depreciation of the United States dollar in foreign 
   124                  exchange markets, or to cooperate with other countries 
   125                  in correcting an international balance-of-payments 
   126                  disequilibrium.
   127  
   128                  5. These senior officials have informed me that 
   129                  fundamental international payments problems within the 
   130                  meaning of section 122 exist and that special import 
   131                  measures to restrict imports are required to address 
   132                  these problems. Specifically, my advisors have 
   133                  determined that an import surcharge in the form of ad 
   134                  valorem duties is required to deal with large and 
   135                  serious United States balance-of-payments deficits. My 
   136                  advisors have also opined that certain products should 
   137                  not be subject to the surcharge because of the needs of 
   138                  the United States economy and that the recommended 
   139                  exceptions are consistent with the limitations of 
   140                  section 122, the purposes of section 122, and the 
   141                  national interest of the United States.
   142  
   143  [[Page 9340]]
   144  
   145                  6. Among other things, I have been informed by my 
   146                  advisors that the United States balance-of-payments 
   147                  position, under any reasonable understanding of the 
   148                  term in the context of section 122, is currently a 
   149                  large and serious deficit. My advisors have studied 
   150                  different methods of evaluating balance-of-payments 
   151                  deficits, including calculations based on current-
   152                  account statistics. In my advisors' opinions, under any 
   153                  of these methods, the United States balance-of-payments 
   154                  position is a large and serious deficit.
   155  
   156                  7. For instance, my advisors have informed me that the 
   157                  United States runs a deficit in selling goods and 
   158                  services overseas, as reported by the United States 
   159                  Bureau of Economic Analysis (BEA) in the ``balance on 
   160                  goods and services''; has recently reflected quarterly 
   161                  deficits in its return on investment or labor, as 
   162                  reported by the BEA in the ``balance on primary 
   163                  income''; and runs a deficit in voluntary transfers, 
   164                  such as remittances, as reported by the BEA in the 
   165                  ``balance on secondary income.'' In other words, the 
   166                  United States runs a trade deficit, does not currently 
   167                  make a net income from the capital and labor that it 
   168                  deploys abroad, and experiences more transfer payments, 
   169                  on net, flowing out of the country than into the 
   170                  country.
   171  
   172                  8. As my advisors have informed me, the United States 
   173                  runs a substantial trade deficit. The large, 
   174                  persistent, and serious annual United States goods 
   175                  trade deficit has grown by over 40 percent in the past 
   176                  5 years alone, reaching $1.2 trillion in 2024. In 2025, 
   177                  the United States goods trade deficit remained at 
   178                  approximately $1.2 trillion. The effects of this 
   179                  deficit are serious, and this deficit contributes to 
   180                  the fundamental international payments problems facing 
   181                  the United States.
   182  
   183                  9. As my advisors have also informed me, the annual 
   184                  balance on the United States primary income turned 
   185                  negative for the first time since at least 1960 in 
   186                  2024. From 1960 to 2023, the United States ran a 
   187                  surplus in its annual balance on primary income. That 
   188                  positive balance on primary income served as a 
   189                  stabilizing force for the United States balance-of-
   190                  payments position even in the face of large and 
   191                  persistent trade deficits. In 2024, however, the 
   192                  balance on primary income turned negative and thus 
   193                  ceased to serve as a counterweight to the trade deficit 
   194                  in the United States current account. Indeed, in 2024, 
   195                  the United States maintained a current account deficit 
   196                  of 4.0 percent of gross domestic product (GDP), almost 
   197                  double the current account deficit of approximately 2.0 
   198                  percent that prevailed between 2013 and 2019, and 
   199                  larger than that which prevailed from 2019 to 2023. As 
   200                  a share of GDP, the staggering deficit of 4.0 percent 
   201                  represented the biggest annual current account deficit 
   202                  since 2008.
   203  
   204                  10. As my advisors have also informed me, the net 
   205                  international-investment position of the United States 
   206                  is in an ongoing decline. According to the BEA, at the 
   207                  end of 2024, the net international-investment position 
   208                  of the United States, as a share of GDP, was negative 
   209                  90 percent, a sharp deterioration from the average of 
   210                  negative 41 percent in the decade between 2010 and 
   211                  2020. In my advisors' view, this is a highly atypical 
   212                  position for a country, particularly the United States. 
   213                  Indeed, both in terms of United States dollars and as a 
   214                  share of GDP, this represents one of the most negative 
   215                  net international-investment positions of any developed 
   216                  country. Because the current account is one of the 
   217                  primary drivers of changes in the net international-
   218                  investment position, the atypically large negative net 
   219                  international-investment position of the United States 
   220                  shows that the United States balance-of-payments 
   221                  deficit is large and serious.
   222  
   223                  11. Further, as my advisors have informed me, the 
   224                  balance on secondary income of the United States has 
   225                  been persistently in a deficit since the 1960s.
   226  
   227                  12. According to my advisors, an import surcharge in 
   228                  the form of ad valorem duties is required to address 
   229                  these fundamental international payments problems. In 
   230                  my advisors' opinions, imposing an import surcharge 
   231                  would deal with the large and serious United States 
   232                  balance-of-payments deficit. My advisors have further 
   233                  recommended that certain products should not be subject 
   234                  to the surcharge because of the needs of the United 
   235                  States economy
   236  
   237  [[Page 9341]]
   238  
   239                  and have opined that a surcharge with certain 
   240                  exceptions would more effectively deal with the 
   241                  balance-of-payments deficit than would a surcharge 
   242                  without the exceptions.
   243  
   244                  13. After considering the information, opinions, and 
   245                  recommendations that have been provided to me by senior 
   246                  officials, among other relevant information and 
   247                  considerations, I find that fundamental international 
   248                  payments problems within the meaning of section 122 
   249                  exist; that those problems significantly harm United 
   250                  States national interests, including economic and 
   251                  national security interests; and that special measures 
   252                  to restrict imports are required to address those 
   253                  problems, as authorized by section 122. Specifically, I 
   254                  find that a surcharge in the form of ad valorem duties 
   255                  on certain imports is required to deal with the United 
   256                  States' large and serious balance-of-payments deficit.

    27  
    28                  By the authority vested in me as President by the 
    29                  Constitution and the laws of the United States of 
    30                  America, including the International Emergency Economic 
    31                  Powers Act (50 U.S.C. 1701 et seq.) (IEEPA), the 
    32                  National Emergencies Act (50 U.S.C. 1601 et seq.), 
    33                  section 604 of the Trade Act of 1974, as amended (19 
    34                  U.S.C. 2483), and section 301 of title 3, United States 
    35                  Code, it is hereby ordered:
    36  
    37                  Section 1. Background. In Executive Order 14193 of 
    38                  February 1, 2025 (Imposing Duties To Address the Flow 
    39                  of Illicit Drugs Across Our Northern Border), as 
    40                  amended; Executive Order 14194 of February 1, 2025 
    41                  (Imposing Duties To Address the Situation at Our 
    42                  Southern Border), as amended; Executive Order 14195 of 
    43                  February 1, 2025 (Imposing Duties To Address the 
    44                  Synthetic Opioid Supply Chain in the People's Republic 
    45                  of China), as amended; Executive Order 14245 of March 
    46                  24, 2025 (Imposing Tariffs on Countries Importing 
    47                  Venezuelan Oil); Executive Order 14257 of April 2, 2025 
    48                  (Regulating Imports With a Reciprocal Tariff To Rectify 
    49                  Trade Practices That Contribute to Large and Persistent 
    50                  Annual United States Goods Trade Deficits), as amended; 
    51                  Executive Order 14323 of July 30, 2025 (Addressing 
    52                  Threats to the United States by the Government of 
    53                  Brazil), as amended; Executive Order 14329 of August 6, 
    54                  2025 (Addressing Threats to the United States by the 
    55                  Government of the Russian Federation), as amended; 
    56                  Executive Order 14380 of January 29, 2026 (Addressing 
    57                  Threats to the United States by the Government of 
    58                  Cuba); and Executive Order 14382 of February 6, 2026 
    59                  (Addressing Threats to the United States by the 
    60                  Government of Iran), I declared or described national 
    61                  emergencies with respect to unusual and extraordinary 
    62                  threats to the national security, foreign policy, or 
    63                  economy of the United States and took actions to deal 
    64                  with those threats, including by imposing, pursuant to 
    65                  IEEPA, additional ad valorem duties on certain imports 
    66                  of certain foreign trading partners.
    67  
    68                  In light of recent events, the additional ad valorem 
    69                  duties imposed pursuant to IEEPA in Executive Order 
    70                  14193, as amended; Executive Order 14194, as amended; 
    71                  Executive Order 14195, as amended; Executive Order 
    72                  14245; Executive Order 14257, as amended; Executive 
    73                  Order 14323, as amended; Executive Order 14329, as 
    74                  amended; Executive Order 14380; and Executive Order 
    75                  14382 shall no longer be in effect and, as soon as 
    76                  practicable, shall no longer be collected. All other 
    77                  actions, including any other action taken to address 
    78                  the national emergencies declared or described in 
    79                  Executive Order 14193, Executive Order 14194, Executive 
    80                  Order 14195, Executive Order 14245, Executive Order 
    81                  14257, Executive Order 14323, Executive Order 14329, 
    82                  Executive Order 14380, and Executive Order 14382, that 
    83                  do not impose additional ad valorem duties under IEEPA 
    84                  or involve steps necessary to implement the imposition 
    85                  of additional ad valorem duties imposed under IEEPA 
    86                  shall not be affected by this order. The national 
    87                  emergencies declared or described in Executive Order 
    88                  14193, Executive Order 14194, Executive Order 14195, 
    89                  Executive Order 14245, Executive Order 14257, Executive 
    90                  Order 14323, Executive Order 14329, Executive Order 
    91                  14380, and Executive Order 14382 or subsequent orders 
    92                  remain in effect and shall not be affected by this 
    93                  order.
    94  
    95                  Sec. 2. Implementation. (a) To effectuate the 
    96                  terminations of the actions described in section 1 of 
    97                  this order, the head of each executive department and 
    98                  agency (agency) is authorized to and shall take all 
    99                  appropriate steps
   100  
   101  [[Page 9438]]
   102  
   103                  to end the additional ad valorem duties imposed under 
   104                  IEEPA in Executive Order 14193, as amended; Executive 
   105                  Order 14194, as amended; Executive Order 14195, as 
   106                  amended; Executive Order 14245; Executive Order 14257, 
   107                  as amended; Executive Order 14323, as amended; 
   108                  Executive Order 14329, as amended; Executive Order 
   109                  14380; and Executive Order 14382. The head of each 
   110                  agency shall immediately begin taking steps to 
   111                  effectuate this order and, as soon as practicable, 
   112                  terminate the collection of the additional ad valorem 
   113                  duties described in section 1 of this order. The head 
   114                  of each agency may, consistent with applicable law, 
   115                  including section 301 of title 3, United States Code, 
   116                  redelegate the authority to take such appropriate steps 
   117                  within the agency.
   118  
   119                      (b) The Secretary of Commerce, the Secretary of 
   120                  Homeland Security, and the United States Trade 
   121                  Representative, as appropriate and in consultation with 
   122                  the Commissioner of U.S. Customs and Border Protection, 
   123                  the Chair of the United States International Trade 
   124                  Commission, and any other senior official they deem 
   125                  appropriate, shall determine whether modifications to 
   126                  the Harmonized Tariff Schedule of the United States are 
   127                  necessary to effectuate this order and may make such 
   128                  modifications through notice in the Federal Register.
   129                      (c) The Executive Order of February 20, 2026 
   130                  (Continuing the Suspension of Duty-Free De Minimis 
   131                  Treatment for All Countries), and the Proclamation of 
   132                  February 20, 2026 (Imposing a Temporary Import 
   133                  Surcharge to Address Fundamental International Payments 
   134                  Problems), are unaffected by this order.
   135                      (d) This order affects only the additional ad 
   136                  valorem duties imposed under IEEPA pursuant to the 
   137                  Executive Orders described in section 1 of this order. 
   138                  This order does not affect any other duties, including 
   139                  duties imposed under section 232 of the Trade Expansion 
   140                  Act of 1962, as amended, 19 U.S.C. 1862, and section 
   141                  301 of the Trade Act of 1974, as amended, 19 U.S.C. 
   142                  2411.
   143

   145                  shall be construed to impair or otherwise affect:
   146  
   147  (i) the authority granted by law to an executive department or agency, or 
   148  the head thereof; or
   149  
   150  (ii) the functions of the Director of the Office of Management and Budget 
   151  relating to budgetary, administrative, or legislative proposals.
   152  
   153                      (b) This order shall be implemented consistent with 
   154                  applicable law and subject to the availability of 
   155                  appropriations.

   161                  enforceable at law or in equity by any party against 
   162                  the United States, its departments, agencies, or 
   163                  entities, its officers, employees, or agents, or any 
   164                  other person.
