    65  
    66                  
    67  Adjusting Imports of Aluminum Into the United 
    68                  States
    69  
    70                  By the President of the United States of America
    71  
    72                  A Proclamation
    73  
    74                  1. On January 19, 2018, the Secretary of Commerce 
    75                  (Secretary) transmitted to me a report on his 
    76                  investigation into the effect of imports of aluminum on 
    77                  the national security of the United States under 
    78                  section 232 of the Trade Expansion Act of 1962, as 
    79                  amended (19 U.S.C. 1862) (section 232). The Secretary 
    80                  found and advised me of the Secretary's opinion that 
    81                  aluminum is being imported into the United States in 
    82                  such quantities and under such circumstances as to 
    83                  threaten to impair the national security of the United 
    84                  States.
    85  
    86                  2. In Proclamation 9704 of March 8, 2018 (Adjusting 
    87                  Imports of Aluminum Into the United States), I 
    88                  concurred in the Secretary's finding that aluminum was 
    89                  being imported into the United States in such 
    90                  quantities and under such circumstances as to threaten 
    91                  to impair the national security of the United States, 
    92                  and decided to adjust the imports of aluminum articles 
    93                  by imposing a 10 percent ad valorem tariff on such 
    94                  articles imported from most countries. Proclamation 
    95                  9704 further stated that any country with which the 
    96                  United States has a security relationship is welcome to 
    97                  discuss alternative ways to address the threatened 
    98                  impairment of the national security caused by imports 
    99                  from that country, and noted that, should the United 
   100                  States and any such country arrive at a satisfactory 
   101                  alternative means to address the threat to the national 
   102                  security such that I determine that imports from that 
   103                  country no longer threaten to impair the national 
   104                  security, I may remove or modify the restriction on 
   105                  aluminum articles imports from that country and, if 
   106                  necessary, adjust the tariff as it applies to other 
   107                  countries, as the national security interests of the 
   108                  United States require.
   109  
   110                  3. In Proclamation 9704, I also directed the Secretary 
   111                  to monitor imports of aluminum articles and inform me 
   112                  of any circumstances that in the Secretary's opinion 
   113                  might indicate the need for further action under 
   114                  section 232 with respect to such imports. Pursuant to 
   115                  Proclamation 9704, the Secretary was authorized to 
   116                  provide relief from the additional duties, based on a 
   117                  request from a directly affected party located in the 
   118                  United States, for any aluminum article determined not 
   119                  to be produced in the United States in a sufficient and 
   120                  reasonably available amount or of a satisfactory 
   121                  quality, or based upon specific national security 
   122                  considerations. Proclamation 9776 of August 29, 2018, 
   123                  and Proclamation 9980 of January 24, 2020, similarly 
   124                  authorized the Secretary to provide relief from certain 
   125                  tariffs on other aluminum products and derivatives set 
   126                  forth in those proclamations.
   127  
   128                  4. In subsequent proclamations, the President adjusted 
   129                  the tariffs applicable to aluminum articles imports 
   130                  from Argentina, Australia, Canada, Mexico, the European 
   131                  Union (EU), and the United Kingdom (UK), after engaging 
   132                  in discussions with each of those parties on 
   133                  alternative ways to address the threat to the national 
   134                  security from such imports.
   135  
   136                  5. The Secretary has informed me that, notwithstanding 
   137                  the 10 percent ad valorem tariff imposed by 
   138                  Proclamation 9704 that mitigated the threatened 
   139                  impairment of our national security, aluminum imports 
   140                  into the United States have continued at unacceptable 
   141                  levels as the global aluminum excess capacity crisis 
   142                  continues. In addition, the exclusion of certain 
   143                  countries
   144  
   145  [[Page 9808]]
   146  
   147                  and products from the tariff and efforts by foreign 
   148                  producers to circumvent the tariff have undermined the 
   149                  purpose of Proclamation 9704, which was to adjust the 
   150                  level of imports of aluminum to remove the threatened 
   151                  impairment of the national security. This has again 
   152                  resulted in aluminum smelter capacity utilization rates 
   153                  in the domestic aluminum industry that are well below 
   154                  the target level recommended in the Secretary's January 
   155                  19, 2018, report. This indicates that the initial 
   156                  tariff of 10 percent ad valorem is not high enough to 
   157                  address the threatened impairment to our national 
   158                  security posed by aluminum imports.
   159  
   160                  6. In particular, the Secretary has informed me that 
   161                  global primary aluminum capacity has continued to 
   162                  increase, fueled by expansions in the People's Republic 
   163                  of China (China) and South America, which is seen in 
   164                  rising aluminum imports that continue to weigh on the 
   165                  price domestic aluminum producers may charge. There has 
   166                  also been a significant increase in Chinese investment 
   167                  in Mexico, driven by massive Chinese government 
   168                  subsidies and the continued ability to exploit 
   169                  loopholes in U.S. trade policy.
   170  
   171                  7. Domestic aluminum producers have been forced to idle 
   172                  additional production and shut down facilities. Two 
   173                  primary aluminum smelters within the United States have 
   174                  closed since Proclamation 9704 was promulgated. In 
   175                  addition, U.S. primary aluminum production decreased by 
   176                  30 percent from 2020 to 2024, and U.S. smelter capacity 
   177                  utilization was only 52 percent in 2024. Overcapacity 
   178                  for primary aluminum has harmed downstream aluminum 
   179                  producers, including producers of aluminum extrusions 
   180                  and aluminum sheet. To allow U.S. aluminum producers to 
   181                  restart production and to incentivize new capacity, 
   182                  additional adjustments to section 232 tariffs on 
   183                  aluminum need to be made, including limiting exemptions 
   184                  and increasing the tariff rate.
   185  
   186                  8. The Secretary has informed me that imports of 
   187                  aluminum articles from countries that are excluded from 
   188                  the tariff regime or have alternative arrangements have 
   189                  remained significantly elevated at levels that once 
   190                  again threaten to impair the national security of the 
   191                  United States. The volume of U.S. imports of aluminum 
   192                  articles from Argentina, Australia, Canada, Mexico, EU 
   193                  countries, and the UK in 2024 was approximately 14 
   194                  percent higher than the average volume of such imports 
   195                  in 2015 through 2017. In particular, the volume of U.S. 
   196                  imports of primary aluminum from Canada in 2024 was 
   197                  approximately 18 percent higher than the average volume 
   198                  for 2015 through 2017. Notwithstanding Proclamation 
   199                  10782 of July 10, 2024, which imposed higher tariffs on 
   200                  certain aluminum imports from Mexico, imports of 
   201                  aluminum from Mexico have continued to surge beyond 
   202                  historical volumes. The volume of U.S. imports of 
   203                  aluminum articles from Mexico in 2024 was approximately 
   204                  35 percent higher than the average volume for 2015 
   205                  through 2017. Proclamation 10782 did not resolve the 
   206                  surge of imports of aluminum from Mexico. Mexican 
   207                  producers are using unfair trade to gain market share 
   208                  in the United States and are leveraging their access to 
   209                  unfairly traded global primary aluminum to do so. I 
   210                  understand that Mexican producers are commingling 
   211                  primary aluminum from China and the Russian Federation 
   212                  (Russia) with primary aluminum from other countries to 
   213                  produce downstream aluminum articles. These practices 
   214                  are distortive and provide continued outlets to absorb 
   215                  the massive amount of global excess capacity and must 
   216                  be remedied. The volume of U.S. imports of primary 
   217                  aluminum from Australia has also surged and in 2024 was 
   218                  approximately 103 percent higher than the average 
   219                  volume for 2015 through 2017. Australia has disregarded 
   220                  its verbal commitment to voluntarily restrain its 
   221                  aluminum exports to a reasonable level.
   222  
   223                  9. These volume increases occurred even though demand 
   224                  for aluminum in the United States and Canada (the 
   225                  market measured by industry) has generally remained 
   226                  flat, averaging about 20 percent since 2018.
   227  
   228                  10. These increasing import volumes support the 
   229                  conclusion that aluminum producers in countries subject 
   230                  to the additional ad valorem tariff proclaimed in 
   231                  Proclamation 9704 are engaging in transshipment or 
   232                  further processing
   233  
   234  [[Page 9809]]
   235  
   236                  of upstream aluminum products in countries that have 
   237                  since been exempted from that tariff. Foreign producers 
   238                  have shifted assembly or manufacturing operations to 
   239                  third countries, such as Mexico. For example, Chinese 
   240                  producers are using Mexico's general exclusion from the 
   241                  tariff to funnel Chinese aluminum to the United States 
   242                  through Mexico while avoiding the tariff.
   243  
   244                  11. The Secretary has informed me that producers in 
   245                  countries that remain subject to the ad valorem tariff 
   246                  have continued to evade the tariff by processing 
   247                  covered aluminum articles into additional downstream 
   248                  derivative products that were not included in the 
   249                  additional ad valorem tariffs proclaimed in 
   250                  Proclamation 9704 and Proclamation 9980. Foreign 
   251                  producers are continuing to expand downstream 
   252                  production to absorb the global excess capacity. 
   253                  Imports of additional derivative aluminum products have 
   254                  increased significantly since the issuance of 
   255                  Proclamation 9704 and Proclamation 9980, eroding the 
   256                  domestic industry's customer base and resulting in 
   257                  depressed demand for aluminum articles produced in the 
   258                  United States.
   259  
   260                  12. The Secretary has also informed me of the impact of 
   261                  the product exclusion process authorized by 
   262                  Proclamation 9704, Proclamation 9776, and Proclamation 
   263                  9980 and implemented by subsequent regulations. This 
   264                  process has resulted in exclusions for a significant 
   265                  volume of imports, in a manner that undermines the 
   266                  purpose of the section 232 measures and threatens to 
   267                  impair the national security of the United States. 
   268                  Certain general approved exclusions remain in effect 
   269                  for entire tariff lines of aluminum imports, 
   270                  notwithstanding the domestic industry's potential to 
   271                  produce many excluded products.
   272  
   273                  13. I determine that these developments and 
   274                  modifications to the original tariff regime as 
   275                  proclaimed in Proclamation 9704 have undermined the 
   276                  regime's national security objectives by preventing the 
   277                  domestic aluminum industry (including derivatives) from 
   278                  achieving sustained production capacity utilization of 
   279                  at least 80 percent, as determined in the Secretary's 
   280                  January 19, 2018, report. I also determine that the 
   281                  modifications failed to achieve their articulated 
   282                  objectives. As a result, I determine that these 
   283                  modifications have resulted in significantly increasing 
   284                  imports of aluminum articles that once again threaten 
   285                  to impair the national security of the United States.
   286  
   287                  14. In light of the Secretary's findings, I have 
   288                  determined that it is necessary and appropriate to 
   289                  adjust the tariff proclaimed by Proclamation 9704, as 
   290                  amended, and the tariff proclaimed by Proclamation 
   291                  9980, as amended, to increase the tariff rate from 10 
   292                  percent ad valorem to 25 percent ad valorem. These 
   293                  actions are necessary and appropriate to remove the 
   294                  threatened impairment of the national security of the 
   295                  United States.
   296  
   297                  15. In light of the Secretary's findings regarding the 
   298                  alternative agreements with Argentina proclaimed in 
   299                  Proclamation 9758 of May 31, 2018; Australia proclaimed 
   300                  in Proclamation 9758; Canada proclaimed in Proclamation 
   301                  9893 of May 19, 2019, and Proclamation 10106 of October 
   302                  27, 2020; Mexico proclaimed in Proclamation 9893 and 
   303                  Proclamation 10782 of July 10, 2024; the European Union 
   304                  proclaimed in Proclamation 10327 of December 27, 2021, 
   305                  and Proclamation 10690 of December 28, 2023; and the 
   306                  United Kingdom proclaimed in Proclamation 10405 of May 
   307                  31, 2022, I have decided that it is necessary to 
   308                  terminate these agreements as of March 12, 2025. As of 
   309                  March 12, 2025, all imports of aluminum articles and 
   310                  derivative aluminum articles from Argentina, Australia, 
   311                  Canada, Mexico, EU countries, and the UK shall be 
   312                  subject to the additional ad valorem tariff proclaimed 
   313                  in Proclamation 9704, as amended, with respect to 
   314                  aluminum articles and Proclamation 9980, as amended, 
   315                  with respect to derivative aluminum articles. Imports 
   316                  of aluminum articles and derivative aluminum articles 
   317                  from Argentina, Australia, Canada, Mexico, EU 
   318                  countries, and the UK shall be subject to the revised 
   319                  tariff rate of 25 percent ad valorem established in 
   320                  clause 2 of this proclamation, commensurate with the 
   321                  tariff rate imposed on such articles imported from most 
   322                  other countries. In my judgment, these modifications 
   323                  are necessary to address the significantly increasing 
   324                  imports of aluminum articles and derivative aluminum 
   325                  articles from these sources, which
   326  
   327  [[Page 9810]]
   328  
   329                  threaten to impair the national security of the United 
   330                  States. Replacing the alternative agreements with the 
   331                  additional ad valorem tariffs will be a more robust and 
   332                  effective means of ensuring that the objectives 
   333                  articulated in the Secretary's January 19, 2018, report 
   334                  and subsequent proclamations are achieved.
   335  
   336                  16. In light of the information provided by the 
   337                  Secretary that the significant increase of imports of 
   338                  certain derivative aluminum articles has depressed 
   339                  demand for aluminum articles produced by domestic 
   340                  aluminum producers, I have determined that it is 
   341                  necessary to adjust the tariff proclaimed in 
   342                  Proclamation 9704 and Proclamation 9980 to apply to 
   343                  additional derivative aluminum articles.
   344  
   345                  17. I have also determined that it is necessary to 
   346                  terminate the product exclusion process as authorized 
   347                  in clause 3 of Proclamation 9704, clause 1 of 
   348                  Proclamation 9776, and clause 2 of Proclamation 9980.
   349  
   350                  18. Section 232, as amended, authorizes the President 
   351                  to take action to adjust the imports of an article and 
   352                  its derivatives that are being imported into the United 
   353                  States in such quantities or under such circumstances 
   354                  as to threaten to impair the national security of the 
   355                  United States.
   356  
   357                  19. Section 604 of the Trade Act of 1974, as amended, 
   358                  authorizes the President to embody in the Harmonized 
   359                  Tariff Schedule of the United States (HTSUS) the 
   360                  substance of statutes affecting import treatment, and 
   361                  actions thereunder, including the removal, 
   362                  modification, continuance, or imposition of any rate of 
   363                  duty or other import restriction.
   364  
   365                  NOW, THEREFORE, I, DONALD J. TRUMP, President of the 
   366                  United States of America, by the authority vested in me 
   367                  by the Constitution and the laws of the United States 
   368                  of America, including section 301 of title 3, United 
   369                  States Code, section 604 of the Trade Act of 1974, as 
   370                  amended, and section 232, do hereby proclaim as 
   371                  follows:
   372  
   373  (1) The provisions of Proclamation 9758 with respect to imports of aluminum 
   374  articles from the Argentina; Proclamation 9758 with respect to imports of 
   375  aluminum articles from the Australia; Proclamation 9893 and Proclamation 
   376  10106 with respect to imports of aluminum articles from Canada; 
   377  Proclamation 9893 and Proclamation 10782 with respect to imports of 
   378  aluminum articles and derivative aluminum articles from Mexico; 
   379  Proclamation 10327 and Proclamation 10690 with respect to imports of 
   380  aluminum articles and derivative aluminum articles from the European Union; 
   381  and Proclamation 10405 with respect to imports of aluminum articles and 
   382  derivative aluminum articles from the United Kingdom shall be ineffective 
   383  as of 12:01 a.m. eastern time on March 12, 2025. The provisions of clause 1 
   384  of Proclamation 9980 as applicable to imports of derivative aluminum 
   385  articles from Argentina, Australia, Canada, and Mexico shall be ineffective 
   386  as of 12:01 a.m. eastern time on March 12, 2025; all imports of aluminum 
   387  articles and derivative aluminum articles from these countries shall be 
   388  subject to the additional ad valorem tariffs proclaimed in Proclamation 
   389  9704, as amended, and Proclamation 9980, as amended. Imports of aluminum 
   390  articles and derivative aluminum articles from Argentina, Australia, 
   391  Canada, Mexico, EU countries, and the United Kingdom will be subject to the 
   392  revised tariff rate of 25 percent ad valorem established in clauses (2) and 
   393  (3) of this proclamation, commensurate with the tariff rate imposed on such 
   394  articles imported from most countries, as amended by this proclamation.
   395  
   396  (2) As of 12:01 a.m. on March 12, 2025, the tariff proclaimed by 
   397  Proclamation 9704, as amended, and the tariff proclaimed by Proclamation 
   398  9980, as amended, are adjusted to increase the respective tariff rates from 
   399  an additional 10 percent ad valorem to an additional 25 percent ad valorem.

  1531  C. Discussion of Comments on Proposed Product Exemptions
  1532  
  1533      USTR received a variety of comments on the proposed exemption list, 
  1534  including support for the products proposed for exemption and requests 
  1535  to remove certain products from the proposed exemption list. 
  1536  Considering the public comments and the advice of the Section 301 
  1537  Committee, as well as the advice of advisory committees and in 
  1538  accordance with the specific direction of the President, the Trade 
  1539  Representative has determined to exempt all of the products proposed 
  1540  for exemption in Annex A to the June 5, 2026 FRN, except the non-
  1541  pharmaceutical applications of certain chemical products. Other than 
  1542  the products with non-pharmaceutical applications, as discussed below, 
  1543  the Trade Representative determined not to remove additional products 
  1544  from the exemption list. The Trade Representative determined to exempt 
  1545  certain additional products not included in the proposed exemptions in 
  1546  Annex A to June 5, 2026 FRN.
  1547  1. Support for Keeping Products on the Proposed Exemption List
  1548      USTR received a number of comments expressing support for 
  1549  maintaining certain proposed exemptions. Comments supported the 
  1550  exemption of coffee, mineral tars, certain copper products, iron 
  1551  oxides, coke, aluminum oxide, and coconut products. Other comments 
  1552  expressed support for maintaining the proposed exemptions from Section 
  1553  301 tariffs for products that are subject to Section 232 tariffs. 
  1554  Commenters generally noted that these products are raw materials with 
  1555  limited-to-no availability from domestic sources or cannot be grown or 
  1556  produced in sufficient quantities or at reasonable prices in the United 
  1557  States or obtained from other sources.
  1558      Considering the public comments and the advice of the Section 301 
  1559  Committee, as well as the advice of advisory committees--and in 
  1560  accordance with the specific direction of the President--the Trade 
  1561  Representative has determined not to remove products other than the 
  1562  non-pharmaceutical applications of certain products from the proposed 
  1563  exemption list, as the remaining products in the proposed exemption 
  1564  list constitute: (1) raw materials that if subject to the proposed 
  1565  additional tariffs could lead to the unavailability of domestic supply; 
  1566  (2) products that could cause economy-wide disruptions if subject to 
  1567  the proposed additional tariffs; (3) products that cannot be grown or 
  1568  produced in sufficient quantities or at reasonable prices in the United 
  1569  States or obtained from other sources; or (4) products for which 
  1570  tariffs may not contribute substantially to the elimination of the 
  1571  acts, policies, and practices found to be actionable.
  1572  2. Determination To Remove Certain Products From the Proposed Exemption 
  1573  List
  1574      Considering the public comments and the advice of the Section 301 
  1575  Committee, as well as the advice of advisory committees--and in 
  1576  accordance with the specific direction of the President--the Trade 
  1577  Representative has determined to limit the exemption for certain 
  1578  chemicals and chemical products to their pharmaceutical applications. 
  1579  Certain comments noted the health-related applications of products 
  1580  proposed for exemptions and stated that certain ingredients that 
  1581  support U.S. manufacturing of healthcare products are not available in 
  1582  the United States in sufficient quantities to meet domestic demand. 
  1583  Some commenters also requested that these product exemptions be limited 
  1584  to their pharmaceutical applications due to competition with domestic 
  1585  production. Limiting exemptions for these proposed chemical products to 
  1586  their pharmaceutical applications is consistent with the proposal in 
  1587  the June 5, 2026 FRN because an exemption for all applications is 
  1588  broader than necessary to cover goods that have limited availability 
  1589  outside of the investigated economies.
  1590  3. Comments Requesting the Removal of Additional Products From 
  1591  Exemption List
  1592      Some commenters requested that USTR remove other products from the 
  1593  proposed exemption list or otherwise advocated for narrowly tailored 
  1594  exemptions. Industries or products for which commenters expressed
  1595  
  1596  [[Page 47331]]
  1597  
  1598  opposition to proposed exemptions include beef, avocados, paprika and 
  1599  paprika products, lithium hexafluorophosphate, and forgings and 
  1600  articles containing forgings.
  1601      Commenters suggested, for example, that beef imported from certain 
  1602  economies is linked to certain acts, policies, and practices found 
  1603  actionable in these investigations, and that exempting these products 
  1604  would benefit foreign exporters of beef produced with forced labor at 
  1605  the expense of the American cattle producer. Similarly, commenters 
  1606  suggested that paprika and paprika derived products, lithium 
  1607  hexafluorophosphate, and certain chemicals used in the production of 
  1608  pesticides are imported from certain economies linked to certain acts, 
  1609  policies, and practices found actionable in these investigations.
  1610      Additionally, commenters suggested that imports of these products 
  1611  are available from domestic sources and are putting pressure on 
  1612  domestic producers. With respect to paprika and paprika derived 
  1613  products, commenters suggested that imports have caused market 
  1614  disruptions, preventing U.S. production of these products. 
  1615  Additionally, comments reported that imports of lithium 
  1616  hexafluorophosphate and certain chemicals used in the production of 
  1617  pesticides have inhibited U.S. production of these products. Commenters 
  1618  pointed to recent and anticipated expansion in U.S. production 
  1619  capabilities, and suggested that imposing tariffs on these products 
  1620  could support investment and employment in domestic production. With 
  1621  respect to forgings and articles containing forgings, commenters 
  1622  suggested that these products are readily available from domestic 
  1623  sources, at reasonable prices, in sufficient quantities and that 
  1624  subjecting imports of these products to tariffs could support 
  1625  investment and employment in the United States. Similarly, comments 
  1626  suggested that the domestic avocado industry is under significant 
  1627  pressure due to low-priced avocado imports and applying tariffs would 
  1628  benefit certain U.S. agricultural producers.
  1629      Considering the public comments and the advice of the Section 301 
  1630  Committee, as well as the advice of advisory committees--and in 
  1631  accordance with the specific direction of the President--the Trade 
  1632  Representative has determined not to remove these products from the 
  1633  list of exempted products. There remains limited availability of these 
  1634  products from domestic sources, a point conceded by one commenter 
  1635  regarding paprika. Regarding claims that these products should be 
  1636  subject to the tariffs because they are related to acts, policies, and 
  1637  practices found actionable in these investigations, Section 
  1638  301(c)(3)(B) provides that the Trade Representative is authorized to 
  1639  take action against any goods or economic sector ``without regard to 
  1640  whether or not such goods or economic sector were involved in the act, 
  1641  policy, or practice that is the subject of such action.''
  1642  
  1643  D. Determination To Exempt Additional Products
  1644  
  1645      In addition to the products initially proposed for exemption in the 
  1646  June 5, 2026 FRN, the Trade Representative, in accordance with the 
  1647  specific direction of the President, has determined in each 
  1648  investigation to exclude an additional 471 products from tariffs 
  1649  imposed with respect to products of that economy. In certain 
  1650  investigations, the Trade Representative also has determined to apply 
  1651  additional exemptions for products from that specific investigated 
  1652  economy based on requested exemptions negotiated in the context of 
  1653  certain agreements and arrangements.
  1654      A number of comments expressed support for product exemptions in 
  1655  addition to the initial list of proposed exemptions in the June 5, 2026 
  1656  FRN. Comments requested exemptions of products including certain 
  1657  agriculture products; metals and alloys; chemicals; semiconductor 
  1658  manufacturing equipment; and art, antique, and collectible products. 
  1659  Certain economies that have concluded ARTs or similar arrangements with 
  1660  the United States have also requested exemption of products negotiated 
  1661  as part of those agreements and arrangements.
  1662      Having considered the public comments, advice of the Section 301 
  1663  Committee, as well as the advice of advisory committees, and the 
  1664  specific direction of the President, the Trade Representative 
  1665  determined to exempt the following additional products from the scope 
  1666  of actions: certain animal products; certain seeds; certain vegetable 
  1667  products; certain sugar and sugar containing products; unflavored 
  1668  instant coffee; certain fertilizer inputs and pesticide inputs; certain 
  1669  animal hides and leather; certain wood products; vanadium oxides and 
  1670  hydroxides; pig iron; certain ferrous inputs and waste; certain 
  1671  aluminum scrap waste; aluminum hydroxide; ash containing precious 
  1672  metals or precious metal compounds; certain battery waste and scrap; 
  1673  certain semiconductor manufacturing equipment; certain pharmaceuticals 
  1674  and pharmaceutical ingredients; worked shell; worn clothing; and 
  1675  certain antiques, collectibles, and art.
  1676      With respect to certain animal products used as food for animals or 
  1677  an input in such food, commenters noted that these products are 
  1678  incorporated into U.S. animal nutrition programs that support 
  1679  livestock, poultry, aquaculture, and pet food production. According to 
  1680  commenters, there is little opportunity for import substitution for 
  1681  these products and any tariff applied to these products would impose 
  1682  additional costs on U.S. consumers.
  1683      With respect to seeds of a kind used for planting, commenters noted 
  1684  that tariffs on seeds have resulted in increased costs for U.S. seed 
  1685  producers and U.S. farmers. According to comments, tariffs that impact 
  1686  seed movement erode the ability of U.S. seed companies to provide U.S. 
  1687  farmers with pure, high-quality seeds at an affordable price due to the 
  1688  global nature of seed production. Specifically, many U.S. seed 
  1689  companies have foreign operations to take advantage of environmental 
  1690  and production conditions, such as additional growing seasons. 
  1691  Commenters also noted that the increased costs associated with seed 
  1692  production could reduce choices in the marketplace for consumers as 
  1693  certain varieties of seed will no longer be viable for 
  1694  commercialization in the United States.
  1695      With respect to certain vegetable products, commenters noted that 
  1696  certain products falling under the relevant HTSUS subheading are 
  1697  already included in Annex A to the June 5, 2026 FRN, but that the 
  1698  proposed product exemptions are limited to products used for religious 
  1699  purposes only. According to comments, products in the relevant HTSUS 
  1700  subheading are essential growing-media and fiber inputs used in nursery 
  1701  production that have no domestic source, including coconut coir, jute 
  1702  burlap, and sisal twine. According to comments, the crops used to 
  1703  produce these products are not commercially grown in the United States 
  1704  given climate limitations and, therefore, there is no domestic industry 
  1705  capable of producing these inputs for the U.S. horticulture sector.
  1706      With respect to in-quota imports of certain sugar and sugar-
  1707  containing products, commenters noted that U.S. sugar producers are 
  1708  more efficient than ever and domestic sugar yields have increased, yet 
  1709  the United States has never produced enough sugar to meet its domestic 
  1710  demand. To meet this demand, the United States has historically had to 
  1711  import significant amounts of sugar. According to comments, U.S. sugar 
  1712  processing
  1713  
  1714  [[Page 47332]]
  1715  
  1716  facilities rely on certain in-quota sugar to meet U.S. demand and 
  1717  supply a critical input of the U.S. food supply chain.
  1718      With respect to unflavored instant coffee, commenters noted that 
  1719  unflavored instant coffee is not available from domestic sources in 
  1720  sufficient quantities for U.S. consumers and coffee companies, 
  1721  including value-added manufacturers. These comments also maintained 
  1722  that over 99 percent of instant coffee imports come from economies 
  1723  covered by these investigations and there are not adequate non-tariffed 
  1724  alternatives. Commenters also noted that U.S. coffee companies will 
  1725  continue to be at a disadvantage producing and innovating ready-to-
  1726  drink and cold brew coffee compared to their foreign competitors if 
  1727  tariffs on unflavored instant coffee are imposed.
  1728      With respect to certain fertilizer inputs and pesticide inputs, 
  1729  commenters noted that imposing additional duties on these chemicals 
  1730  could cause disruptions or shortages in the domestic supply due to the 
  1731  limited availability of certain active ingredients outside of the 
  1732  investigated economies and because these products cannot be produced in 
  1733  the United States in sufficient quantities to meet domestic demand. 
  1734  Commenters also noted that the exemptions would be essential to avoid 
  1735  tariff inversion, causing U.S. manufacturers who produce value-added 
  1736  products to be disadvantaged in comparison to importers of finished 
  1737  agriculture chemical products.
  1738      With respect to certain animal hides and leather products,

  1741  there is no domestic supply. According to commenters, tariffs would

  1744      With respect to certain wood and wood products, commenters noted

summary.text: Analyzing trade policy statements for accuracy regarding tariff exemptions and duty caps across regions.Identifying discrepancies between effective dates and missing proclamation references in the annex amendments.Flagging new inconsistencies in scope overrides, in-transit exceptions, and annex description changes.Identifying a date-counting inconsistency in the suspension period and effective-date recitals.Enumerating additional textual discrepancies across effective dates, scope clauses, and annex references.Extending the discrepancy list with naming, rate description, and in-transit mode mismatches.Applying DATES in-transit and effective-date rules to entry and withdrawal scenarios.Mapping economy-specific exemptions in Note52(j) and flagging unverifiable image-list rules.Calculating equivalent ad valorem rates and applying country-specific caps for duty layers across scenarios.Extending the duty calculation to severability and FTZ admission timing under the import date rule.

Q1.answer: (a) Proclamation 11046, FR Doc. 2026-14991, 91 FR 46639, signed 20 July 2026, published 23 July 2026: imposes 50% on Annex II Canadian alcoholic beverages; operative clause (1) applies to goods entered for consumption, or withdrawn from warehouse for consumption, on/after 12:01 a.m. ET 19 Aug. 2026 as printed. (b) 11047, 2026-14992, 91 FR 46653, signed 20 July, published 23 July: same for dairy Annex II, 19 Aug. entry/withdrawal. (c) 11048, 2026-14997, 91 FR 46663, signed 20 July, published 23 July: same for motor vehicles Annex II, 19 Aug. entry/withdrawal. (d) 11056, 2026-17294, 91 FR 54789, signed 18 Aug., filed 21 Aug., published 24 Aug.: clause (1) moves effective date to 12:01 a.m. 22 Aug. 2026 for all three, by amending Annex II chapeaux; event is the original entry/withdrawal event. (e) 11061, 2026-18835, 91 FR 58311, signed 8 Sept., filed 11 Sept., published 14 Sept.: alcohol import ban, clause (1) applies to goods imported on/after 12:01 a.m. 29 Sept. (importation, not entry). (f) 11062, 2026-18836, 91 FR 58319, same dates: dairy ban, imported on/after 29 Sept. (g) 11063, 2026-18837, 91 FR 58325, same dates: motor-vehicle ban, imported on/after 29 Sept. (h) 11064, 2026-18838, 91 FR 58331, same dates: alcohol scope, Annex I Part A added / Part B removed, entered/withdrawn on/after 12:01 a.m. 15 Sept. (i) 11065, 2026-18839, 91 FR 58339, same dates: motor-vehicle scope, Part A added / Part B removed, entered/withdrawn on/after 15 Sept. (j) 11076, 2026-22292, 91 FR 68861, signed 23 Oct., filed 29 Oct., published 30 Oct.: motor vehicles further scope, Annex I Part A removed / Part B added, entered/withdrawn on/after 12:01 a.m. 30 Oct. Product-group changes: Alcohol - 11046 Annex II, then 11064 Part A/B, then 11061 Annex changes duty to ban for imports on/after 29 Sept. Dairy - 11047 Annex II, then 11062 Annex ban; no dairy scope proclamation is in the Federal Register list through 14 Nov. Motor vehicles - 11048 Annex II, then 11065 Part A/B, then 11063 Annex ban, then 11076 Part A removed/Part B added.
Q1.basis: Search for section 338 Canada proclamations returned the 10 documents above with numbers, citations, signed/published dates. Operative clauses: 11046 cl.(1),(3) 91 FR 46641; 11047 cl.(1) 91 FR 46654-46655; 11048 cl.(1) 91 FR 46665; 11056 cl.(1) 91 FR 54790; 11061 cl.(1)-(2) 91 FR 58312-58313; 11062 cl.(1)-(2) 91 FR 58320; 11063 cl.(1)-(2) 91 FR 58326; 11064 cl.(1)-(2) 91 FR 58332; 11065 cl.(1)-(2) 91 FR 58340; 11076 cl.(1)-(2) 91 FR 68862. Filed stamps at end of each FR Doc.
Q1.uncertainty: Annex product lists are images and not readable; group changes are stated from operative Part A/B and Annex references, not from image contents. No dairy scope proclamation was found; 11062 cl.(3) nevertheless refers to one - see Q11.

Q2.answer: (a) Each $40,000. Entry 1, 20 Aug. 2:00 p.m.: $40,000 x 50% = $0 owed - before effective date. Entry 2, 21 Aug. 11:59 p.m.: $0. Entry 3, 22 Aug. 12:01 a.m.: $40,000 x 50% = $20,000. (b) Original 11046 para.9 and cl.(1),(3) print 19 Aug. (91 FR 46640-46641). 11056 cl.(1) provides the effective date 'shall be 12:01 a.m. eastern time on August 22, 2026' and amends only 'the chapeau of Annex II of each of Proclamations 11046, 11047, and 11048' by deleting 19 Aug. and inserting 22 Aug. (91 FR 54790). It does not expressly amend the body text of cl.(1)/(3) or para.9 of the originals. The conflict is resolved in practice by 11056's operative first sentence, its cl.(2) direction to suspend collection, and later recitals (e.g. 11061 para.4) stating duties became effective 22 Aug.; the later, specific suspension governs over the unamended printed date. (c) Entry 1: 11056 cl.(4) - 'To the extent that implementation of this proclamation requires a refund of duties collected, refunds shall be processed pursuant to applicable law and CBP's standard procedures for such refunds' (91 FR 54791); cl.(2) directs agencies to suspend collection as soon as practicable. No automatic refund amount/date is stated. (d) No further presidential action was needed to begin: the original proclamations themselves imposed the duties; 11056 moved the effective date, and later proclamations state the suspension lapsed and duties became effective 22 Aug. without a new imposition (11061 paras.3-4, 91 FR 58311). (e) Section 338, as recited in 11046 para.10 (91 FR 46640-46641), permits duties 'not to take effect earlier than 30 days after the President's proclamation finding...' The finding proclamation was signed 20 July 2026; 20 July + 30 days = 19 Aug. 2026 (11 days remaining in July to 31 July, plus 19 days in August).
Q2.uncertainty: The documents do not expressly state that body cl.(1)/(3) of the originals is superseded as against the Annex chapeau amendment; the reading above is the most defensible reconciliation and is confirmed by later recitals. Refund mechanics beyond cl.(4) are left to applicable law/CBP procedures.

Q3.answer: (a) Each $30,000, MFN free. A. Arrives 10 Sept., entered 14 Sept.: may be imported; imported before 29 Sept., so 11061 cl.(2) retains 50% duty: $30,000 x 50% = $15,000. B. Arrives 27 Sept., warehouse withdrawal 5 Oct.: may be imported (imported before 29 Sept.); withdrawn after, but cl.(2) applies to products 'imported, but not yet entered...or withdrawn...prior to September 29' - read with cl.(1) (ban on goods imported on/after 29 Sept.), the 27 Sept. import is not banned; duty $15,000 on withdrawal. C. Arrives 11:30 p.m. 28 Sept., entry 29 Sept. 9:00 a.m.: may be imported (imported before 12:01 a.m. 29 Sept.); duty $15,000. Entry date after the ban date does not trigger the ban, which is measured by importation. D. Arrives 12:30 a.m. 29 Sept.: imported on/after 12:01 a.m. 29 Sept., excluded from importation under 11061 cl.(1); may not be imported, so no consumption-entry duty arises. (b) E: admitted to FTZ 25 Sept. - after the 22 Aug. effective date, so under 11046 cl.(4) it must be admitted as privileged foreign status (unless domestic-status eligible); it was imported before 29 Sept., so not banned; on entry for consumption 6 Oct. the 50% duty applies ($30,000 x 50% = $15,000 on the assumed value). (c) If the ban is held invalid as applied, 11061 cl.(9)(b): 'the 50 percent ad valorem duty imposed in Proclamation 11046 shall apply to the import to which the invalidated import ban...had applied before its invalidation' - so post-ruling imports of this beer bear $15,000 (50%) duty. (d) No: 11061 cl.(3) - besides changing Annex products from duty to ban, the proclamation 'does not otherwise affect the products...that are subject to the additional ad valorem duties imposed in Proclamation 11046' as modified by the alcohol scope proclamation; non-Annex products remain dutiable as before.
Q3.basis: 11061 cl.(1)-(3) and cl.(9)(b) 91 FR 58312-58313; 11046 cl.(4) 91 FR 46641 (FTZ privileged foreign status on/after effective date).
Q3.uncertainty: Shipment E's value is not stated; $15,000 assumes the same $30,000 value. The FTZ clause wording ('subject upon entry...to any ad valorem rate...related to classification') is imprecise; cl.(2) of 11061 supplies the 50% rate for pre-29 Sept. imports.

Q4.answer: Each $100,000; 232 stated as 25% on full value = $25,000 each. (a) 10 Sept. 2026 (before 15 Sept. scope): X (alcohol): 232 $25,000, 338 $0. Y (dairy): 232 $25,000, 338 $0. Z (motor): 232 $25,000, 338 $0. (b) 1 Oct. 2026 (after 15 Sept.): X: 232 $25,000, 338 50% x $100,000 = $50,000. Y: 232 $25,000, 338 $0 - no dairy scope proclamation changes the original exclusion. Z: 232 $25,000, 338 $50,000. (c) Original exclusion: 'The duties imposed in this proclamation shall not apply to articles subject to duties pursuant to section 232...' 11046 cl.(2), 91 FR 46641; 11047 cl.(2), 91 FR 46655; 11048 cl.(2), 91 FR 46665. Override for alcohol/motor: 'The duties imposed pursuant to Proclamation 11046, as modified in this proclamation, shall apply in addition to duties imposed pursuant to section 232...effective...on or after 12:01 a.m. eastern time on September 15, 2026' 11064 cl.(1), 91 FR 58332; same for motor vehicles 11065 cl.(1), 91 FR 58340.
Q4.basis: Clauses cited in (c) above; scope effective date 15 Sept. 12:01 a.m. ET in 11064/11065 cl.(1)-(2).
Q4.uncertainty: None on readable text for X and Z. For Y, the absence of a dairy scope proclamation is a search result through 14 Nov. 2026; 11062 cl.(3) refers to a dairy scope proclamation that was not found (see Q11).

Q5.answer: (a) P (Sept. Part A, not original): 14 Sept. 3 p.m. $0 (before 15 Sept.); 15 Sept. 12:01 a.m. 50% applies; 29 Oct., 30 Oct., 3 Nov. 50% applies. Q (original Annex II + Sept. Part B): 14 Sept. 50% applies (original duty); 15 Sept. onward $0 - Part B 'shall no longer be subject' from 15 Sept. R (original + Oct. Part A): 14 Sept., 15 Sept., 29 Oct. 50% applies; 30 Oct. 12:01 a.m. and 3 Nov. $0 - Oct. Part A removes the duty from 30 Oct. S (Oct. Part B, not earlier): 14 Sept., 15 Sept., 29 Oct. $0; 30 Oct. 12:01 a.m. and 3 Nov. 50% applies. (b) Oct. scope (11076): signed 23 Oct. 2026 (91 FR 68861), filed 29 Oct. 2026 at 11:15 a.m. (FR Doc. stamp, 91 FR 68871), published 30 Oct. 2026; applies from 12:01 a.m. ET 30 Oct. 2026, cl.(1)-(2) (91 FR 68862). Scope proclamations apply only to goods entered/withdrawn on or after that time - they do not reach earlier entries, and contain no refund provision (cl.(1)-(8) contain no refund clause, unlike 11056 cl.(4)). (c) Waiting period as recited: 'not to take effect earlier than 30 days after the President's proclamation finding...' (11048 para.9, 91 FR 46664; repeated in scope proclamations para.8/9). P: signed 8 Sept., dutiable 15 Sept. = 7 days after signing, but 57 days after the original 20 July finding. S: signed 23 Oct., dutiable 30 Oct. = 7 days after signing, 102 days after the original finding. The scope proclamations recite the 30-day rule but do not explain how a 7-day interval fits it; they frame the change as modifying duties already imposed, not as a new finding, but that reasoning is not stated in the text.
Q5.basis: 11065 cl.(1)-(2) 91 FR 58340 (Part A subject, Part B no longer, 15 Sept.); 11076 cl.(1)-(2) 91 FR 68862 (Part A no longer, Part B subject, 30 Oct.); 11076 signature/filed stamp 91 FR 68862, 68871; waiting-period recitals 11048 para.9, 11065 para.8, 11076 para.9.
Q5.uncertainty: How the 30-day rule is satisfied for new Part A/B products is not explained in the scope proclamations; the dates above are arithmetic from the original finding. No refund language exists in the scope proclamations.

Q6.answer: (a) $100,000, MFN 4% = $4,000 MFN duty. (1) Switzerland: 12.5% net - 301 = (12.5%-4%) x $100,000 = $8,500; MFN+301 = $12,500. (2) Norway: 12.5% flat - 301 $12,500; total $16,500. (3) United Kingdom: 10% flat - 301 $10,000; total $14,000. (4) Germany (EU): 10% net - 301 = 6% x $100,000 = $6,000; total $10,000. (5) Taiwan: 10% net - 301 $6,000; total $10,000. (6) Türkiye: 12.5% flat - 301 $12,500; total $16,500. (7) Japan: 12.5% net - 301 $8,500; total $12,500. (8) Liechtenstein: not among the 60 investigated economies - 301 $0; total $4,000 (MFN only). (9) Hong Kong, China: 12.5% flat - 301 $12,500; total $16,500. (10) India: 10% flat - 301 $10,000; total $14,000. (b) 301 only: Germany MFN 12%: MFN >=10% cap, 301 $0. Japan MFN 12%: (12.5%-12%) x $100,000 = $500. Taiwan MFN exactly 10%: >=cap, $0. South Korea MFN exactly 10%: (12.5%-10%) x $100,000 = $2,500. Switzerland MFN free: 12.5% x $100,000 = $12,500. (c) Differ from June proposal (flat 10% or 12.5%, no netting): Switzerland, Germany (EU), Taiwan, Japan - net-of-MFN treatment added; India - rate changed 12.5% to 10%. Norway, UK, Türkiye, Hong Kong, Liechtenstein do not differ in rate treatment (UK was already 10%; Liechtenstein was not investigated). Reason stated for India's change (and the other six economies): after the June proposal, India (with Cambodia, Guatemala, Honduras, Sri Lanka, Trinidad and Tobago) imposed a forced-labor import ban, so it was moved to the 10% rate to encourage effective enforcement (Memorandum 91 FR 47720; final Notice 91 FR 47319).
Q6.basis: Memorandum sec.1(a) 91 FR 47720 (10% list; EU/Taiwan 10% net; Japan/Korea/Switzerland 12.5% net; all other 12.5%); final Notice sec.II.A 91 FR 47320-47321 and specific determinations (EU 91 FR 47323, Japan 91 FR 47324, Switzerland/Taiwan 91 FR 47327, South Korea 91 FR 47327); 60-economy list Memorandum 91 FR 47717-47718 (no Liechtenstein); June proposal summary 91 FR 34272-34274 (flat 10%/12.5%, no netting).
Q6.uncertainty: Economy-specific exemption Parts (image annexes) are assumed not to cover these generic products, per scenario assumptions; rates above are the economy rates before any (j) exemption.

Q7.answer: (a) France (EU), 3 cents/kg x 2,000 kg = $60 MFN duty; equivalent rate $60/$12,000 = 0.5%; cap 10%, so 301 = (10%-0.5%) x $12,000 = $1,140. (b) MFN duty: 4% x $20,000 = $800 plus 25c x 4,000 = $1,000, total $1,800; equivalent 9%. Italy (EU, cap 10%): 301 = 1% x $20,000 = $200. Japan (cap 12.5%): 301 = 3.5% x $20,000 = $700. Brazil (flat 12.5%, not a net economy): 301 = 12.5% x $20,000 = $2,500. (c) Column 1 duty $2,200/$20,000 = 11% equivalent. Taiwan (cap 10%): equivalent >=10%, 301 $0. Switzerland (cap 12.5%): 301 = (12.5%-11%) x $20,000 = $300. (d) The non-ad-valorem rule is in new U.S. Note 52(k), Annex I to USTR Notice 2026-15181, 91 FR 47364: for EU, Japan, South Korea, Switzerland and Taiwan goods subject to a specific or compound Column 1-General rate, the ad valorem equivalent is column 1 duty payable divided by customs value (with the 50c/$10 = 5% example). The at/above-cap result is in the last two sentences of Note 52(k) (91 FR 47364) for headings 9903.05.39/9903.05.76 (10% economies) and 9903.05.49/9903.05.71/9903.05.74 (12.5% economies), and in Memorandum sec.1(a)(ii) 91 FR 47720: where MFN is greater than or equal to the cap, the section 301 tariff is zero.
Q7.basis: Note 52(k) 91 FR 47364; Memorandum sec.1(a)(ii) 91 FR 47720; final Notice sec.II.A 91 FR 47320-47321 (caps by economy).
Q7.uncertainty: None; Brazil is not listed in Note 52(k), so no equivalent-rate netting applies to it.

Q8.answer: (a) Dominican Republic, $80,000, MFN free, 12.5% flat rate = $10,000 if the duty applies. 1. Loaded 22 July, entered 29 July: $10,000 - in-transit exception requires entry before 12:01 a.m. 28 July. 2. Entered 27 July 3:00 p.m.: $0 - loaded before 24 July and entered before 28 July. 3. Entered 28 July 12:01 a.m.: $10,000 - 'before 12:01 a.m. on July 28' is not met at 12:01 a.m. 4. Loaded 24 July 6:00 a.m., entered 27 July: $10,000 - not loaded before 12:01 a.m. 24 July. 5. Entered 23 July: $0 - before the 24 July effective date. 6. Warehouse withdrawal 26 July: $10,000 - withdrawal on/after 24 July is covered; a warehoused arrival is not goods in transit on the final mode. 7. Air freight loaded 23 July 9:00 p.m., entered 25 July: $10,000 - the exception by its terms covers goods 'loaded onto a vessel', not an aircraft. (b) The in-transit rule is stated in the DATES line of USTR Notice 2026-15181, 91 FR 47318. (c) Memorandum signed 23 July 2026 (91 FR 47717, 47723); duties applicable from 12:01 a.m. ET 24 July 2026 (DATES line, 91 FR 47318); published 28 July 2026 (Memorandum 91 FR 47717; Notice 91 FR 47318). (d) Patented pharmaceutical article in 9903.04.62: entered 30 July 2026: $10,000 (12.5% x $80,000) - the pharma exemption in Annex I.B is effective 31 July; entered 3 Aug. 2026: $0 - Annex I.B, effective for goods entered on/after 12:01 a.m. 31 July, adds patented pharmaceutical articles (9903.04.60-9903.04.66) to the 9903.05.90 exclusion in Note 52(f)(8) (91 FR 47394).
Q8.basis: DATES line 91 FR 47318; Dominican Republic determination, final Notice 91 FR 47323 (12.5%); Annex I.B 91 FR 47394; Note 52(f)(8) as inserted 91 FR 47394.
Q8.uncertainty: Whether 'vessel' in the DATES line is intended to include aircraft is not stated; the literal reading is applied and flagged. Warehouse goods' original loading date is not given; the answer treats warehoused goods as not 'in transit'.

Q9.answer: (a) Thailand (12.5%): Note 52(a) - for 9802.00.80 the duty applies to the assembled value less U.S. products: ($100,000 - $35,000) x 12.5% = $8,125. (b) Israel repairs (12.5%): for 9802.00.50 the duty applies to the value of repairs: $6,000 x 12.5% = $750. (c) Mexico (10%): (i) USMCA free entry: $0 - Note 52(h) (heading 9903.05.55) exempts Mexico goods entered free under USMCA. (ii) No USMCA claim: 10% x $50,000 = $5,000. (d) Japan passenger car under 9903.94.01: $0 - Note 52(f)(2) excludes passenger vehicles provided for in 9903.94.01 from the 301 duties. (e) Brazil, 232 heading not mentioned in Note 52(f): $100,000 x 12.5% = $12,500 - Note 52(f) excludes only the enumerated 232 headings; an unlisted 232 heading remains subject to 301 in addition (Note 52(a)). (f) June proposal: exempted 'all articles and parts currently subject to section 232 tariffs' plus informational materials, donations and accompanied baggage (June Notice 91 FR 34274; summarized in final Notice 91 FR 47318). Adopted text: Note 52(f) excludes only articles provided for in the enumerated 232 headings (9903.82, 9903.94, 9903.76, 9903.74, 9903.79 series, 91 FR 47362-47363); Note 52(a) exempts only products for personal use in accompanied baggage (91 FR 47352). The readable adopted Note 52 contains no general informational-materials or donations exemption.
Q9.basis: Note 52(a) 9802 rules 91 FR 47352; Note 52(f)(1)-(7) 91 FR 47362-47363; Note 52(g)-(h) 91 FR 47363; June Notice sec.IV 91 FR 34274.
Q9.uncertainty: Informational materials/donations might appear in the image-only Annex A list under Note 52(b); on the readable text there is no such general exemption, and per scenario assumptions image lists are not applied unless named.

Q10.answer: Scenario 1, extrusions $200,000, MFN 3% = $200,000 x 3% = $6,000. (a) 10 Sept.: MFN $6,000 + section 232 50% x $200,000 = $100,000 + section 338 $0 (232 exclusion, scope not yet effective) + section 301 $0 (9903.82.02 exclusion) = $106,000 total. (b) 16 Sept.: MFN $6,000 + 232 $100,000 + 338 50% x $200,000 = $100,000 (scope effective 15 Sept., in addition to 232) + 301 $0 = $206,000. Scenario 2, rye whisky $60,000, MFN free. (c) 1 Sept. USMCA entry: 338 50% x $60,000 = $30,000; 301 $0 - Canada goods entered free under USMCA are exempt under Note 52(g); total $30,000. 338 has no USMCA exemption in its readable text. (d) 1 Sept. no USMCA claim: 338 $30,000 + 301 Canada 10% x $60,000 = $6,000; total $36,000. (e) Arrives 2 Oct.: 2 Oct. is on/after 29 Sept., so under 11061 cl.(1) it is excluded from importation; it may not be imported for consumption, so no 338/301 duty is payable on a consumption entry - the ban, not a duty, applies. (f) IEEPA northern-border duties: EO 14193 as amended imposed 25%, later 35%, but EO 14389 of 20 Feb. 2026, FR Doc. 2026-03832, 91 FR 9437-9438, provides the IEEPA duties in EO 14193 as amended, EO 14257 as amended etc. 'shall no longer be in effect and, as soon as practicable, shall no longer be collected.' The 10% temporary surcharge, Proclamation 11012, 2026-03824, 91 FR 9339, cl.(7), applied 24 Feb. 2026 through 12:01 a.m. 24 July 2026 (150 days, cl.13/para.17, 91 FR 9341-9342); September entries are after expiry, and in any event cl.(4) and para.14(k),(l) exclude 232 articles and USMCA Canada/Mexico goods. Neither duty applies in September 2026.
Q10.basis: 11048 cl.(2) 91 FR 46665 and 11065 cl.(1) 91 FR 58340 (338 in addition to 232 from 15 Sept.); USTR Notice 2026-15181 Note 52(f)(1) 91 FR 47362 (aluminum 9903.82.02 excluded from 301) and Note 52(g) 91 FR 47363 (Canada USMCA exemption); 11061 cl.(1)-(2) 91 FR 58312-58313; EO 14389 sec.1-2, 91 FR 9437-9438; Proclamation 11012 cl.(4),(7), para.14, 91 FR 9341-9343.
Q10.uncertainty: MFN in Scenario 1 is stated as 3% in the question; $6,000 is shown for completeness though the question asks for additional layers. Whether the whisky is on any image-only 301 exemption list is assumed not, per scenario assumptions.

Q11.answer: Each discrepancy is listed once. (1) Effective date: 11046 para.9 and cl.(1),(3) print 19 Aug. (91 FR 46640-46641); 11056 cl.(1) says effective date 'shall be' 22 Aug. and amends only the Annex II chapeau (91 FR 54790); 11061 para.1, 91 FR 58311, repeats 'effective August 19, 2026' while para.4 of the same document says duties 'became effective' 22 Aug. (2) Suspension length: 11056 paras.4-5 and cl.(1) describe a 3-day suspension moving 19 to 22 Aug.; signed 18 Aug., 3 days later would be 21 Aug., yet 11061 para.4 says suspension 'lapsed' at 12:01 a.m. 22 Aug. (3) Scope of amendment in 11056: cl.(1) first sentence changes the effective date generally, second sentence amends only 'the chapeau of Annex II'; original cl.(1) and cl.(3) of 11046-11048 stating 19 Aug. are not expressly amended. (4) 232 stacking: original 11046-11048 cl.(2) 'shall not apply to articles subject to duties pursuant to section 232' (91 FR 46641); 11064/11065 cl.(1) say modified duties 'shall apply in addition to duties imposed pursuant to section 232' (91 FR 58332, 58340) without expressly amending cl.(2). (5) Dairy scope reference: 11062 cl.(3), 91 FR 58320, refers to 'the Proclamation of September 8, 2026 (Modifying the Scope...With Respect to Dairy)'; no such proclamation appears in the Federal Register search/list - only alcohol (11064) and motor-vehicle (11065) scope proclamations. (6) Forced-labor findings: June Notice 2026-11296, 91 FR 34273-34274, lists 54 economies that failed to impose and effectively enforce and 6 (Canada, Ecuador, EU, Indonesia, Mexico, Pakistan) that failed only to effectively enforce, then concludes 'all...have failed both'; USTR Notice 2026-15181, 91 FR 47318, repeats the 54/6 split and then 'all...have failed to satisfy both factors' (91 FR 47318). (7) Textile mechanism rate in proposal: Memorandum 2026-15274, 91 FR 47719, says the proposal would allow textiles to enter 'at a zero section 301 tariff rate'; June Notice 2026-11296, 91 FR 34274, and final Notice 91 FR 47318, say 'at a reduced Section 301 tariff rate' - the Memorandum misdescribes the proposal. (8) TRQ timing: Memorandum recital, 91 FR 47720, 'establishing these TRQs is not feasible at this time, but...will be feasible by September 1, 2026'; operative sec.2, 91 FR 47721, requires establishment only 'as soon as the Trade Representative determines that it is feasible', with no 1 Sept. date; final Notice repeats 'when feasible' (91 FR 47321). (9) In-transit rule: final Notice DATES, 91 FR 47318, excepts goods loaded on a vessel before 12:01 a.m. 24 July and entered before 12:01 a.m. 28 July; Annex I Note 52(a), 91 FR 47352, imposing duties on goods entered on/after 24 July contains no in-transit exception in its readable text. (10) Exclusion description: 11061 cl.(3), 91 FR 58313, says the proclamation changes products 'from being subject to...duties...to being subject to the import ban' and does not otherwise affect them; cl.(2) retains the 50% duty for Annex products imported before 29 Sept. - the description omits that retained duty.
Q11.basis: All citations are to operative clauses, recitals and DATES lines in FR Docs. 2026-14991, 2026-17294, 2026-18835, 2026-18836, 2026-18838, 2026-18839, 2026-15274, 2026-11296 and 2026-15181 at the pages given. Image-only annex content was not used.
Q11.uncertainty: Matters on which documents are merely silent, and image-only lists, are not listed. Whether an in-transit or informational-materials rule appears in an image annex cannot be determined from the readable text.

Q12.answer: All entries 10 Sept. 2026, after 301 effective date. Rates: Cambodia, Malaysia, Bangladesh, Argentina, Indonesia, Mexico, El Salvador 10% flat; Taiwan 10% net; Japan 12.5% net; Thailand 12.5% flat; Italy (EU) 10% net. (a) Aloe etc. 1302.19.91, $60,000, MFN free: Cambodia $0 - Note 52(j)(5)(ii)(C) exempts this article for Cambodia; Malaysia 10% x $60,000 = $6,000 - Malaysia list in (j)(4) is Psyllium, Boswellia, Argan only. (b) Boswellia 1301.90.91, $100,000, MFN free: Malaysia $0 under (j)(4)(ii)(B); Taiwan $0 under (j)(10)(ii)(B); Bangladesh 10% x $100,000 = $10,000 - Bangladesh list (j)(9) is Psyllium and Argan only; Argentina 10% = $10,000 - Argentina list (j)(8) is Psyllium, Aloe, Argan only. (c) Argan oil 1515.90.81, $100,000, MFN 4%: Taiwan $0 under (j)(10)(ii)(D); Japan: MFN 4% <12.5%, 301 = 8.5% x $100,000 = $8,500 (no Japan-specific list); Indonesia 10% flat x $100,000 = $10,000 (Indonesia list (j)(11) is Aloe only). (d) Sesame seeds for sowing 1207.40.00, $50,000, MFN 2%: $0 for Japan, Mexico and Thailand - Note 52(c)(4) exempts sesame seeds for sowing for all economies. (e) Psyllium 1211.90.89, $40,000: Cambodia (MFN free) $0 under (j)(5)(ii)(A); Thailand (MFN free) 12.5% x $40,000 = $5,000; El Salvador (MFN free) 10% x $40,000 = $4,000 - El Salvador list (j)(7) is Aloe only; Italy MFN 2%: EU net 10%, 301 = (10%-2%) x $40,000 = $3,200.
Q12.basis: USTR Notice 2026-15181: rate determinations sec.II.A, 91 FR 47320-47321 and specific determinations at 91 FR 47321-47327; Note 52(c)(4) 91 FR 47363; Note 52(j)(4)-(11) 91 FR 47364-47385, in particular (j)(4)(ii) Malaysia, (j)(5)(ii) Cambodia, (j)(7)(ii) El Salvador, (j)(8)(ii) Argentina, (j)(9)(ii) Bangladesh, (j)(10)(ii) Taiwan, (j)(11)(ii) Indonesia. Italy is an EU member state; EU determination 91 FR 47323 imposes 10% net of MFN.
Q12.uncertainty: EU/Italy economy-specific list in Note 52(j)(2) is an image; per scenario assumptions the product is on no image list, so no (j) exemption is applied. The same assumption applies to general image lists in Note 52(b).

Q13.answer: Machine $200,000, MFN free unless stated; Annex I-C, June Proclamation 11032 cl.(2) applies 8 June-31 Dec. 2027. (a) Canada USMCA, U.S. parts $60,000: non-U.S. content $140,000 x 25% = $35,000; effective 17.5% > 15% floor, so $35,000. (b) No U.S. content: $200,000 x 25% = $50,000. (c) No USMCA qualification: cl.(2)(d) inapplicable, $200,000 x 25% = $50,000. (d) Japan, MFN 2.5%: cl.(2)(b) Japan listed, MFN+232 =15%, so 232 = (15%-2.5%) x $200,000 = $25,000. (e) U.S. parts $20,000, plus $30,000 U.S.-smelted aluminum in a Canada-made part: (d) counts only parts produced in the U.S. ($20,000), non-U.S. content $180,000 x 25% = $45,000; cl.(2)(c) 10% 'entirely' test fails because most metal by weight was melted/smeared outside the U.S. (cl.(4) requires at least 85% U.S. by weight, 91 FR 34088), so $45,000. (f) 6 Oct. 2026, same as (e): $45,000 - no readable change between 6 and 20 Oct. affects Annex I-C cl.(2). (g) U.S. parts $140,000: non-U.S. $60,000 x 25% = $15,000, but cl.(2)(d) floor: total effective duty shall not be less than 15% x $200,000 = $30,000, so $30,000. (h) Cl.(2) treatment applies until 11:59 p.m. EST 31 Dec. 2027 (cl.(2), 91 FR 34087); from 12:01 a.m. EST 1 Jan. 2028 cl.(3)(a) applies the rates in cl.(3) of Proclamation 11021 (Annex I-C articles revert to the April 2026 Annex I-A/B framework - 50% for aluminum/steel articles, 25% for derivatives, subject to its 10% U.S.-metal rule).
Q13.basis: Proclamation 11032, 2026-11314, cl.(2)(a)-(d) 91 FR 34087, cl.(3) 91 FR 34088, cl.(4) 85% weight test 91 FR 34088; background para.2, 91 FR 34085 (50% articles, 25% derivatives, 15% fixed machinery under 11021). Annex IV detail is an image; cl.(2)(d) text itself states the 15% floor.
Q13.uncertainty: Annex IV (image) may contain additional calculation detail for the 15% floor; on the readable text the floor is applied as a minimum effective 232 duty of 15% of customs value. The 2028 rate for this specific Annex I-C article depends on its classification under 11021 cl.(3), whose annex lists are images.

Q14.answer: (1) Partly correct: recital says TRQs 'will be feasible by September 1, 2026' (Memorandum 91 FR 47720) but operative sec.2 requires establishment 'as soon as...feasible' (91 FR 47721) - no deadline is given. (2) Incorrect for the proposed-action round: over 450 comments and nearly 60 witnesses were on the March initiation (June Notice 91 FR 34273); on the June proposal USTR received over 1,600 comments and heard over 100 witnesses (Memorandum 91 FR 47719; final Notice 91 FR 47319). (3) Partly correct: seven economies moved to 10%, but six adopted a ban (Cambodia, Guatemala, Honduras, India, Sri Lanka, Trinidad and Tobago) and Jordan undertook an ART commitment, not a ban (Memorandum 91 FR 47720; final Notice 91 FR 47319). (4) Incorrect: commenters urged removing beef, avocados, paprika etc.; USTR 'determined not to remove these products' (final Notice 91 FR 47331, sec.III.C.3). (5) Incorrect: net-of-MFN economies are EU, Taiwan, Japan, South Korea, Switzerland (Memorandum sec.1(a)(ii)); only EU (Part C), Switzerland (Part D) and Taiwan (Part K) have economy-specific Parts - Japan and South Korea have only Part A (specific determinations 91 FR 47324, 47327). (6) Partly correct: USTR excluded 'an additional 471 products' in each investigation (91 FR 47331); it exempted 'certain sugar and sugar-containing products' and in-quota sugar, not all sugar (91 FR 47331). (7) Incorrect: capping at 10%/12.5% applies only to net-of-MFN economies; flat-rate economies bear MFN plus 10%/12.5% (Memorandum sec.1(a); final Notice 91 FR 47320-47321). (8) Correct: a product subject to the duty admitted to a FTZ 'only may be admitted as privileged foreign status', except products eligible for domestic status (final Notice 91 FR 47321). (9) Correct: if an exemption is held invalid, 'the applicable tariff action...would apply to imports...to which the invalidated exemption...applied before its invalidation' (Memorandum sec.4(e), 91 FR 47723; final Notice sec.IV, 91 FR 47335). (10) Correct: USTR exempted all Annex A proposed products 'except the non-pharmaceutical applications of certain chemical products' and 'determined not to remove additional products' (final Notice 91 FR 47330, sec.III.C).
Q14.basis: Memorandum 2026-15274 91 FR 47717-47778; June Notice 2026-11296 91 FR 34272; final Notice 2026-15181 91 FR 47318-47335, at pages cited in the answer.
Q14.uncertainty: None on the readable text; '471 products' is stated per investigation, not as a single aggregate list, and the annex lists themselves are images.

Q15.answer: Customs value $100,000 each; amounts below are additional duties only (MFN excluded). Case N = no USMCA; Case U = USMCA-qualified and claimed. (1) 10 Feb. 2025: N: IEEPA $0 (paused until 4 Mar., EO 14197), 232 $0 (Canada exempt under alternative agreement until 12 Mar., Proc.10895 cl.(1)), reciprocal/surcharge/301/338 not yet in force; total $0. U: same $0. (2) 6 Mar. 2025: N: IEEPA 25% x $100,000 = $25,000 (effective 4 Mar.); 232 $0 - Canada still exempt until 12 Mar., and stacking EO 14289 (retroactive to 4 Mar.) bars 232 where IEEPA applies; total $25,000. U: same $25,000 - USMCA exemption in EO 14231 is effective 7 Mar., so not available 6 Mar. (3) 10 Mar. 2025: N: IEEPA $25,000; 232 $0 (Canada exempt until 12 Mar.); total $25,000. U: IEEPA $0 (USMCA exemption effective 7 Mar.); 232 $0 (Canada exempt until 12 Mar.); total $0. (4) 14 Mar. 2025: N: IEEPA $25,000; 232 $0 by non-stacking (IEEPA bars 232, EO 14289 sec.3(a)(ii) as originally in force); total $25,000. U: IEEPA $0 (USMCA); 232 25% x $100,000 = $25,000 (Proc.10895 cl.(2), effective 12 Mar.); total $25,000. (5) 3 June 2025: N: IEEPA $25,000; 232 25% = $25,000 but non-stacking bars it; total $25,000. U: IEEPA $0; 232 $25,000; total $25,000. Proc.10947 increase to 50% is effective 4 June, not 3 June. (6) 10 June 2025: both N and U: 232 50% x $100,000 = $50,000 (Proc.10947 cl.(1)-(2), effective 4 June); IEEPA $0 in N by amended stacking (232 bars IEEPA, Proc.10947 cl.(5)) and $0 in U by USMCA exemption; total $50,000. (7) 5 Aug. 2025: both: 232 $50,000; IEEPA rate is 35% from 1 Aug. (EO 14325 sec.2) but barred by stacking in N and exempt in U; total $50,000. (8) 2 Mar. 2026: both: 232 $50,000; IEEPA/reciprocal terminated 20 Feb. 2026 (EO 14389); surcharge (from 24 Feb.) excluded for 232 articles; total $50,000. (9) 10 June 2026: both: 232 50% under Proc.11021 Annex I-A, cl.(2) (effective 6 Apr. 2026), $50,000; surcharge $0 (232 exclusion); IEEPA terminated; total $50,000. (10) 27 July 2026: both: 232 $50,000; 301 $0 - Canada 10% duty excludes aluminum 9903.82.02, Note 52(f)(1); surcharge expired 24 July; total $50,000. (11) 25 Aug. 2026: both: 232 $50,000; 338 $0 - original cl.(2) excludes 232 articles; 301 $0 as above; total $50,000. (12) 14 Sept. 2026: both: 232 $50,000; 338 $0 - scope Proc.11065 effective 15 Sept., not yet; total $50,000. (13) 16 Sept. 2026: both: 232 $50,000 + 338 50% (Proc.11065 cl.(1), in addition to 232) = $50,000; 301 $0; total $100,000. (14) 10 Nov. 2026: both: same as (13), $100,000 - Oct. scope Proc.11076 does not list these extrusions (assumed on no Part A/B list). Other additional duties then in force on Canadian products - IEEPA (terminated Feb. 2026), reciprocal (terminated Feb. 2026), section 122 surcharge (expired 24 July 2026 and 232-excluded), 301 (9903.82.02-excluded) - are $0 for the reasons stated; section 338 is $0 until 15 Sept. for the 232 reason.
Q15.basis: EO 14193 sec.2 90 FR 9114; EO 14197 sec.3 90 FR 9183 (pause to 4 Mar.); EO 14231 sec.2 90 FR 11785 (USMCA from 7 Mar.); Proc.10895 cl.(1)-(2) 90 FR 9810-9811 (Canada 232 from 12 Mar., 25%); EO 14289 sec.3 90 FR 18908 (non-stacking, retroactive to 4 Mar.); Proc.10947 cl.(1)-(2),(5) 90 FR 24200-24201 (50% and stacking reversal from 4 June); EO 14325 sec.2 90 FR 37958 (35% from 1 Aug.); EO 14389 sec.1-2 91 FR 9437-9438 (termination); Proc.11012 cl.(4),(7) 91 FR 9342-9343 (surcharge to 24 July 2026, 232-excluded); Proc.11021 cl.(1)-(2) 91 FR 18203-18204 (50% Annex I-A from 6 Apr. 2026); USTR Notice Note 52(f)(1) 91 FR 47362; Proc.11048 cl.(2) 91 FR 46665; Proc.11065 cl.(1) 91 FR 58340.
Q15.uncertainty: Whether Canada's pre-12 Mar. 2025 aluminum alternative agreement exempted these extrusions is taken from Proc.10895 cl.(1) terminating the Canada provisions; the scenario assumption that they are 'within' the 232 aluminum duties is read as classification, not as negating that country exemption. Image annexes (9903 headings, 232 annex lists) are not readable; heading 9903.82.02 is given in the scenario.
